subject: Operating Systems
question_text:
Consider a computer system with multiple shared resource types, with one instance per resource type. Each instance can be owned by only one process at a time. Owning and freeing of resources are done by holding a global lock (L). The following scheme is used to own a resource instance:
 function OWNRESOURCE(Resource R) 
    Acquire lock L // a global lock 
    if R is available then 
        Acquire R        
        Release lock L 
    else
        if R is owned by another process P then        
        Terminate P, after releasing all resources owned by P        
        Acquire R        
        Restart P        
        Release lock L        
        end if
    end if    
end function

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
explanation:
On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control:

1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction.
2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off.
3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR.

Answer: (iii), (i), (ii)

subject: Compiler Design
topic: Data Flow Analysis (Live Variables, Reaching Definitions)
question_text: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?
options: (A) Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables.
(B) Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree.
(C) Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase.
(D) Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase.
explanation:
Checking each statement about the symbol table:

- It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs.
- It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations.
- It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized.
- "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

Answer: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" is FALSE.

subject: Compiler Design
question_text: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
explanation:
Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment.

Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

Answer: Register assignment to variables

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
[latex]g(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex], [latex]f(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]B[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex], and their composition defined as [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] is a mapping from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex].
If [latex]f(. )[/latex] and [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function [latex]g(. )[/latex]?
options: (C) [latex]g(. )[/latex] must be a bijective function, that is, both one-to-one and onto.
(D) [latex]g(. )[/latex] is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.
explanation:
We're told [latex]f[/latex] is onto (B→C) and the composite [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about [latex]g[/latex] (A→B).

Intuitively: since [latex]f[/latex] alone is already onto [latex]C[/latex], every element of [latex]C[/latex] has some preimage in [latex]B[/latex] regardless of [latex]g[/latex]. The fact that [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is also onto just says [latex]g[/latex]'s image happens to hit enough of [latex]B[/latex] to cover all of [latex]f[/latex]'s "useful" preimages — but [latex]g[/latex] itself doesn't need to be onto all of [latex]B[/latex] (there could be elements of [latex]B[/latex] entirely outside [latex]g[/latex]'s range, as long as [latex]f[/latex] still reaches every element of [latex]C[/latex] through the range [latex]g[/latex] does cover), nor does [latex]g[/latex] need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of [latex]A[/latex] could map to the same element of [latex]B[/latex]).

A simple counterexample confirms it: let [latex]B=\{1,2\}[/latex], [latex]C=\{1\}[/latex], [latex]f[/latex] onto, and [latex]g[/latex] mapping every element of [latex]A[/latex] to just [latex]1\in B[/latex] — [latex]g[/latex] is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is trivially onto.

Answer: g(.) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

subject: Algorithms
question_text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and [latex]T[/latex] be a minimum spanning tree of [latex]G[/latex]. For any two vertices, [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex], let [latex]d_1(u, v)[/latex] and [latex]d_2(u, v)[/latex] be the shortest distances between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex], respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible [latex]G[/latex], [latex]T[/latex], [latex]u[/latex], and [latex]v[/latex]?
explanation:
[latex]T[/latex] is a subgraph of [latex]G[/latex] using only a subset of [latex]G[/latex]'s edges, so any path that exists inside [latex]T[/latex] between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] is also a valid path in [latex]G[/latex] (with the exact same total weight). This means the shortest path in [latex]G[/latex] can never be longer than the shortest path in [latex]T[/latex] — [latex]G[/latex] has strictly more routing options available (all of [latex]T[/latex]'s edges, plus possibly more), so it can only match or beat [latex]T[/latex]'s best distance.

So [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex] always holds (equality is common but not guaranteed — a shortcut through a non-tree edge in [latex]G[/latex] can make [latex]d_1[/latex] strictly smaller).

Answer: [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex]

subject: Algorithms
question_text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

[latex]T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n \quad \text{for} \quad n > 0, \quad T(0) = 1[/latex]

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
explanation:
[latex]T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]. Substitute [latex]T(n)=2^nS(n)[/latex]:
[latex]2^nS(n)=2\cdot2^{n-1}S(n-1)+n2^n=2^nS(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]
Dividing through by [latex]2^n[/latex]: [latex]S(n)=S(n-1)+n[/latex].

Unrolling this simple recurrence: [latex]S(n)=S(0)+\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=1+\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

So [latex]T(n)=2^n\cdot\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex]

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text: Consider the following [latex]B^+[/latex] tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?
options: (A) None of the nodes will split.
(B) At least one node will split and redistribute.
(C) The total number of nodes will remain same.
(D) The height of the tree will increase.
explanation:
Inserting a new key into a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than [latex]3[/latex]), it must split into two leaves, pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent.

Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of [latex]3[/latex] keys before inserting [latex]23[/latex], it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level. Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here.

Answer: At least one node will split and redistribute; and the height of the tree will increase.

subject: Computer Networks
question_text: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
explanation:
TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet:

- P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet).
- P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake).
- P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests).

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1)

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question_text:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

[latex]x + k y = 1[/latex]
[latex]k x + y = -1[/latex]
options: (A) There is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the above system of equations has no solution.
(B) There exist an infinite number of values of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has no solution.
(C) There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
(D) There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.
explanation:
[latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex].

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

subject: Digital Logic
question_text: Let [latex]X[/latex] be a 3-variable Boolean function that produces output as '1' when at least two of the input variables are '1'. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where [latex]a, b, c, d, e[/latex] are Boolean variables?
options: (A) [latex]X(a, b, X(c, d, e)) = X(X(a, b, c), d, e)[/latex]
(B) [latex]X(a, b, X(a, b, c)) = X(a, b, c)[/latex]
(C) [latex]X(a, b, X(a, c, d)) = (X(a, b, a) \text{ AND } X(c, d, c))[/latex]
(D) [latex]X(a, b, c) = X(a, X(a, b, c), X(a, c, c))[/latex]
explanation:
[latex]X[/latex] is the 3-input majority function: [latex]X(p,q,r)=1[/latex] iff at least [latex]2[/latex] of [latex]p,q,r[/latex] are [latex]1[/latex]. A useful fact: whenever two of the three inputs to [latex]X[/latex] are the same variable [latex]v[/latex], the output is forced to equal [latex]v[/latex] regardless of the third input (e.g. [latex]X(v,v,\text{anything})=v[/latex]).

Checking [latex]X(a,b,X(a,b,c))=X(a,b,c)[/latex]: let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex], then [latex]m=a[/latex] too, and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,a,a)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex], then (since one of [latex]a,b[/latex] is [latex]0[/latex] and the other [latex]1[/latex]) [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,b,c)=m[/latex]. Either way it checks out. True.

Checking [latex]X(a,b,c)=X(a,X(a,b,c),X(a,c,c))[/latex]: note [latex]X(a,c,c)=c[/latex] (two matching inputs). Let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex]: [latex]m=a[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,a,c)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex]: [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,c,c)=c=m[/latex]. Checks out both ways. True.

The other two options can be shown false with a direct counterexample assignment of [latex]a,b,c,d[/latex] (the two sides disagree for some input combination) — they do not hold as general identities.

Answer: X(a,b,X(a,b,c)) = X(a,b,c); and X(a,b,c) = X(a, X(a,b,c), X(a,c,c))

question_text: The number [latex]-6[/latex] can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2's complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2's complement representation(s) of [latex]-6[/latex]?
explanation:
Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension: replicate the sign bit (here, the leading [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]-6[/latex] is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits.

[latex]-6[/latex] in 4-bit: [latex]1010[/latex].
Correct 8-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1010[/latex] (four [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,1010[/latex] incorrectly prepends [latex]1000[/latex] instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong.
Correct 16-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1111\,1111\,1010[/latex] (twelve [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,0000\,0000\,1010[/latex] is similarly wrong.

Answer: 1111 1010 (8-bit) and 1111 1111 1111 1010 (16-bit)

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?
options: (A) The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is [latex](n - 1)[/latex].
(B) An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
(C) Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2 n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
(D) Every BST is also a Min-Heap.
explanation:
Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers:

- Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total.
- Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape.
- Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order.

question_text: A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where [latex]RA[/latex], [latex]RB[/latex], and [latex]RZ[/latex] are 32-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown?
options: (A) The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.
(B) The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
(C) The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.
(D) The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
explanation:
The given data path consists of:

- Two 32-bit registers: RA and RB.
- Two multiplexers (Mux_A and Mux_B).
- Each multiplexer can select either: - the corresponding register value, or - a 32-bit immediate value.
- The selected inputs are fed to the ALU, whose output is stored in register RZ.

Thus, the ALU can receive the following combinations of operands:

Mux_A Mux_B Operands
RA RB Two registers
RA Immediate One register + one immediate
Immediate RB One immediate + one register
Immediate Immediate Two immediate values

Now, evaluate each statement.

Option A: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.

Since Mux_A can select RA and Mux_B can select RB, the ALU can perform operations such as [latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + RB [/latex]

Hence, Option A is Correct.

Option B: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
Examples:
[latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + 10 [/latex] or [latex] RZ \leftarrow 20 + RB [/latex]
Therefore, Option B is Correct.

Option C: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values. Both multiplexers can independently select their immediate inputs. Therefore, the ALU can perform operations like [latex] RZ \leftarrow 15 + 25 [/latex]
Hence, Option C is Correct.

Option D: The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value. This is false because the data path also supports:
- Register + Register
- Immediate + Immediate
- Register + Immediate

Therefore, Option D is Incorrect.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
options: (A) [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
(B) [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
(C) There exists a DFA with [latex]\leq 2^n[/latex] states that accepts [latex]L[/latex].
(D) Every DFA that accepts [latex]L[/latex] has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states.
explanation:
For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist.

- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement.
- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false).
- "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false.
- "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement.

question_text: Let [latex]S[/latex] be the set of all ternary strings defined over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex]. Consider all strings in [latex]S[/latex] that contain at least one occurrence of two consecutive symbols, that is, "aa", "bb" or "cc". The number of such strings of length 5 that are possible is _______. (Answer in integer)
explanation:
Total ternary strings of length [latex]5[/latex] over [latex]\{a,b,c\}[/latex]: [latex]3^5=243[/latex].

It's easier to count the complement: strings with no two consecutive equal symbols anywhere. The first symbol has [latex]3[/latex] choices; each subsequent symbol just needs to differ from its immediate predecessor, giving [latex]2[/latex] choices each time: [latex]3\times2^4=3\times16=48[/latex] such "no-repeat" strings.

So strings containing at least one consecutive repeat [latex]=243-48=195[/latex].

Answer: 195

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question_text:
Consider the given function [latex]f(x)[/latex].

[latex]f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + b & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x^3 + x^2 + 1 & \text{for } x \geq 1 \end{cases}[/latex]

If the function is differentiable everywhere, the value of [latex]b[/latex] must be ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation:
For [latex]f[/latex] to be differentiable at [latex]x=1[/latex], it must first be continuous there, and then have matching one-sided derivatives.

Continuity: left-hand value [latex]=a(1)+b=a+b[/latex]; right-hand value [latex]=1^3+1^2+1=3[/latex]. So [latex]a+b=3[/latex].

Matching derivatives: left derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(ax+b)=a[/latex]. Right derivative [latex]=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+x^2+1)=3x^2+2x[/latex], evaluated at [latex]x=1[/latex]: [latex]3+2=5[/latex]. So [latex]a=5[/latex].

Substituting back: [latex]b=3-a=3-5=-2[/latex].

Answer: -2.0

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text: A box contains 5 coins: 4 regular coins and 1 fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability [latex]P(\text{head}) = 0.5[/latex] and for a fake coin, [latex]P(\text{head}) = 1[/latex]. You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
explanation:
By Bayes' theorem, [latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{P(HH\mid\text{fake})P(\text{fake})}{P(HH)}[/latex].

[latex]P(HH\mid\text{fake})=1\times1=1[/latex] (fake coin always shows heads). [latex]P(HH\mid\text{regular})=0.5\times0.5=0.25[/latex].
[latex]P(\text{fake})=\dfrac15[/latex], [latex]P(\text{regular})=\dfrac45[/latex].

[latex]P(HH)=1\times\dfrac15+0.25\times\dfrac45=0.2+0.2=0.4[/latex].

[latex]P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.50

question_text: The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node. Suppose a Min-Heap [latex]T[/latex] stores 32 keys. The height of [latex]T[/latex] is _____________. (Answer in integer)

Level [latex]0[/latex] holds [latex]1[/latex] node, level [latex]1[/latex] holds [latex]2[/latex], level [latex]2[/latex] holds [latex]4[/latex], level [latex]3[/latex] holds [latex]8[/latex], level [latex]4[/latex] holds [latex]16[/latex] — cumulatively [latex]1+2+4+8+16=31[/latex] nodes fill levels [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]4[/latex] completely. subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text: Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the tag values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, 1K = [latex]2^{10}[/latex], 1M = [latex]2^{20}[/latex].]
explanation:
Cache [latex]=16\text{K}=2^{14}[/latex] bytes, block size [latex]=16=2^4[/latex] bytes, so number of cache lines [latex]=\dfrac{2^{14}}{2^4}=2^{10}[/latex] — index field [latex]=10[/latex] bits, offset field [latex]=4[/latex] bits.

Main memory [latex]=1\text{M}=2^{20}[/latex] bytes, byte-addressable, so the address is [latex]20[/latex] bits wide. Tag field [latex]=20-10-4=6[/latex] bits per line.

Total bits needed to store all tag values [latex]=6\text{ bits}\times2^{10}\text{ lines}=6\times2^{10}[/latex].

Answer: 6×2^10

question_text:
A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
explanation:
With [latex]64=2^6[/latex] registers, each register-number field needs [latex]6[/latex] bits. With [latex]50[/latex] distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits (since [latex]2^5=32<50\le64=2^6[/latex]).

The instruction [latex]\text{ADD R1, \#25}[/latex] (meaning [latex]\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25[/latex]) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the [latex]32[/latex]-bit instruction splits as: opcode ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] one register field ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] immediate field (the rest).

Immediate field width [latex]=32-6-6=20[/latex] bits.

Answer: 20

topic: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority)
question_text:
A computer has two processors, [latex]M_1[/latex] and [latex]M_2[/latex]. Four processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4[/latex] with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

[latex]M_1[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
[latex]M_2[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_2[/latex] and [latex]P_1[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process [latex]P_i[/latex] is scheduled to a processor [latex]M_k[/latex], if the processor is free and no other process [latex]P_j[/latex] is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?
explanation:
All four processes arrive together at [latex]t=0[/latex] with two free processors, so two of them start immediately. Since [latex]P_1[/latex] is [latex]M_1[/latex]'s top priority and [latex]P_2[/latex] is [latex]M_2[/latex]'s top priority (and conveniently each is the other machine's lowest priority, so there's no conflict), the natural non-conflicting start is [latex]P_1\to M_1[/latex] and [latex]P_2\to M_2[/latex], both beginning at [latex]t=0[/latex].

[latex]P_2[/latex] (burst [latex]16[/latex]) finishes first, at [latex]t=16[/latex], freeing [latex]M_2[/latex]. Among the still-waiting [latex]P_3,P_4[/latex], [latex]M_2[/latex]'s priority order ([latex]P_2{>}P_3{>}P_4{>}P_1[/latex]) favors [latex]P_3[/latex], so [latex]P_3[/latex] starts on [latex]M_2[/latex] at [latex]t=16[/latex], running until [latex]16+25=41[/latex].

[latex]P_1[/latex] (burst [latex]20[/latex]) finishes next, at [latex]t=20[/latex], freeing [latex]M_1[/latex]. Only [latex]P_4[/latex] remains waiting, so it starts on [latex]M_1[/latex] at [latex]t=20[/latex], running until [latex]20+10=30[/latex].

Waiting times: [latex]P_1{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_2{:}\,0[/latex], [latex]P_3{:}\,16-0=16[/latex], [latex]P_4{:}\,20-0=20[/latex].

Average [latex]=\dfrac{0+0+16+20}{4}=\dfrac{36}{4}=9[/latex].

Answer: 9

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text:
Consider two relations describing teams and players in a sports league:

[latex]teams(tid, tname):tid, tname [/latex] are team-id and team-name, respectively
[latex]players(pid, pname, tid):pid,pname,tid[/latex] denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having name as 'MI'?
options: (A) [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t ( t \in teams \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
(B) [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \wedge \exists t ( t \in players \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
(C) [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t ( t \in teams \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
(D) [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \wedge \exists t ( t \in players \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
explanation:
We want, for each player [latex]p[/latex] in [latex]\text{players}[/latex], their name, restricted to only those players whose [latex]tid[/latex] matches some team [latex]t[/latex] in [latex]\text{teams}[/latex] with [latex]t.tname=\text{'MI'}[/latex].

This is exactly:
[latex]\{p.pname\mid p\in players\ \wedge\ \exists t(t\in teams\ \wedge\ p.tid=t.tid\ \wedge\ t.tname=\text{'MI'})\}[/latex]

The key correctness checks: the outer variable [latex]p[/latex] must range over [latex]players[/latex] (not [latex]teams[/latex], since we want player names), and the join condition [latex]p.tid=t.tid[/latex] must actually be present inside the existential (options that drop this join condition would incorrectly return every player's name whenever team 'MI' exists at all, regardless of which team the player is actually on).

Answer: {p.pname | p∈players ∧ ∃t(t∈teams ∧ p.tid=t.tid ∧ t.tname='MI')}

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Subnet Address} & \textbf{Subnet Mask (in CIDR notation)} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 145.36.0.0 & /16 & E1 \\ \hline 145.36.128.0 & /17 & E2 \\ \hline 145.36.64.0 & /18 & E3 \\ \hline 145.36.255.0 & /24 & E4 \\ \hline \text{Default} & -- & E5 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
explanation:
Routers use longest-prefix matching: find every subnet entry that contains the destination address, and among those, forward via the one with the most specific (longest) prefix.

Destination: [latex]145.36.109.70[/latex]. Check each entry:
- [latex]145.36.0.0/16[/latex] (E1): matches any [latex]145.36.x.x[/latex] — matches.
- [latex]145.36.128.0/17[/latex] (E2): covers 3rd octet [latex]128[/latex]-[latex]255[/latex]; our 3rd octet is [latex]109[/latex] — no match.
- [latex]145.36.64.0/18[/latex] (E3): covers 3rd octet [latex]64[/latex]-[latex]127[/latex]; [latex]109[/latex] falls in this range — matches.
- [latex]145.36.255.0/24[/latex] (E4): only [latex]145.36.255.x[/latex]; no match.

Between the two matches (E1's [latex]/16[/latex] and E3's [latex]/18[/latex]), the [latex]/18[/latex] is more specific (longer prefix), so it wins.

Answer: E3

question_text:
Let [latex]A[/latex] be a 2x2 matrix as given:
[latex]A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right][/latex]
What are the eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]A^{13}[/latex]?

Find the eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] from its characteristic equation:

If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of [latex]A[/latex], then [latex]\lambda^{13}[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvalue of [latex]A^{13}[/latex] (eigenvalues of a matrix power are just the original eigenvalues raised to that power):
[latex](\sqrt2)^{13}=2^{13/2}=2^{6}\cdot2^{1/2}=64\sqrt2[/latex], and similarly [latex](-\sqrt2)^{13}=-64\sqrt2[/latex].

Answer: 64√2, -64√2

Let [latex]d(u, v)[/latex] denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]V[/latex]. Let the maximum value of [latex]d(u, v)[/latex], [latex]u, v \in V[/latex] such that [latex]u \neq v[/latex], be 30. Let [latex]T[/latex] be any breadth-first-search tree of [latex]G[/latex]. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph [latex]G[/latex]?
options: (C) The height of [latex]T[/latex] is at least 15.
(D) The height of [latex]T[/latex] is at least 30.
explanation:
Let the diameter of the graph be the maximum shortest distance between any two vertices.
It is given that [latex] \max_{u,v\in V,\;u\ne v} d(u,v)=30. [/latex]
Thus, the diameter of the graph is 30.

Relation between BFS Tree Height and Graph Diameter

A Breadth-First Search (BFS) tree rooted at a vertex (r) has the following property:

- The level of every vertex equals its shortest distance from the root.
- Therefore, the height of the BFS tree is the maximum shortest distance from the root to any vertex, which is called the eccentricity of the root.

Let the height of the BFS tree be (h). Then, [latex] h=\max_{v\in V} d(r,v). [/latex]

Using the Diameter

Let the diameter of the graph be (D=30). A well-known property of graphs is [latex] \text{Radius} \ge \left\lceil\frac{D}{2}\right\rceil. [/latex]

Since [latex] D=30, [/latex] we get [latex] \left\lceil\frac{30}{2}\right\rceil=15. [/latex]

Every vertex has eccentricity at least the radius. Hence, regardless of the chosen BFS root, [latex] h\ge 15. [/latex]

The height need not be exactly 15 or exactly 30. It can be any value between 15 and 30 depending on the chosen root.

For example:

- If the BFS starts from a central vertex, the height can be 15.
- If it starts from an end vertex of a diameter, the height can be 30.

Correct Answer: (C) The height of (T) is at least 15.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b\}[/latex]:

[latex]L_1 = \{ \alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a, b\}^+ \text{ and } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \{ \alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a\}^+ \text{ and } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}[/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: (B) [latex]L_1[/latex] is a regular language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is not a regular language.
(C) [latex]L_1[/latex] is not a regular language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a regular language.
(D) Neither [latex]L_1[/latex] nor [latex]L_2[/latex] is a regular language.
explanation:
[latex]L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}[/latex] (α completely unrestricted): checking membership genuinely requires comparing an arbitrary-length prefix against an arbitrary-length suffix for exact equality. For instance, "[latex]abbaab[/latex]" is in [latex]L_1[/latex] (via [latex]\alpha=ab,\beta=ba[/latex]) even though its very first and very last characters differ — so no bounded "look at a few characters" trick works; a finite automaton cannot carry the unbounded memory needed to remember an arbitrarily long prefix for later comparison. This is the same style of argument used to show languages like [latex]\{ww\}[/latex] are non-regular. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not regular.

[latex]L_2=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha\in\{a\}^+,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}[/latex] (α restricted to all-a's): here, since [latex]\alpha[/latex] consists only of [latex]a[/latex]'s, we can always just use the shortest valid split ([latex]|\alpha|=1[/latex]): any string of length [latex]\ge3[/latex] that starts with [latex]a[/latex] and ends with [latex]a[/latex] can always be decomposed as (first character [latex]a[/latex]) + (everything in between, as [latex]\beta[/latex]) + (last character [latex]a[/latex]). So [latex]L_2[/latex] is exactly "strings of length [latex]\ge3[/latex] starting and ending with [latex]a[/latex]," which is simply matched by the regular expression [latex]a(a|b)^+a[/latex]. [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular.

Answer: L1 is not regular but L2 is regular.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex], where [latex]m[/latex] and [latex]n[/latex] are natural numbers:

[latex]L_1 = \{ a^m b^m c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \{ a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1 \}[/latex]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: (B) [latex]L_1[/latex] is a context-free language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is not a context-free language.
(C) [latex]L_1[/latex] is not a context-free language but [latex]L_2[/latex] is a context-free language.
explanation:
[latex]L_1=\{a^mb^mc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: this requires two separate comparisons tied to the same value [latex]m[/latex] — matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s exactly (using up a stack), and independently comparing the [latex]c[/latex]-count against that same [latex]m[/latex] again. A single-stack PDA can only "remember and compare" one running count at a time; once the stack is used up matching [latex]a[/latex]'s against [latex]b[/latex]'s, the value of [latex]m[/latex] is no longer available to compare against the [latex]c[/latex]'s. This mirrors the classic non-context-free pattern [latex]a^nb^nc^n[/latex]. [latex]L_1[/latex] is not context-free.

[latex]L_2=\{a^mb^nc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}[/latex]: here the [latex]c[/latex]-count only needs to match the combined total of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s (not two separate comparisons). A single stack handles this easily: push one symbol for every [latex]a[/latex] and every [latex]b[/latex] (treating them the same way), then pop one symbol per [latex]c[/latex], accepting if the stack empties exactly when the input ends. [latex]L_2[/latex] is context-free.

Answer: L1 is not context-free but L2 is context-free.

subject: Compiler Design
question_text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing [latex]First[/latex] and [latex]Follow[/latex] during top-down parsing by a compiler?
options: (A) For a production [latex]A \to \epsilon ,  \epsilon [/latex] will be added to [latex]First(A) [/latex].
(B) If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to[latex] First(S) [/latex], where [latex] S [/latex] is the start symbol.
(C) For a production [latex] A \to \epsilon,  \epsilon [/latex] will be added to [latex] Follow(A) [/latex].
(D) If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to [latex] Follow(S) [/latex], where [latex] S [/latex] is the start symbol.
explanation:
Standard rules for computing [latex]\text{First}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets:

- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to First(A)": TRUE — this is exactly the base rule for handling nullable productions in First-set computation.
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to First(S)": FALSE — the end marker [latex]\$[/latex] belongs in [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets (marking "nothing more can follow"), never in a [latex]\text{First}[/latex] set.
- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to Follow(A)": FALSE — [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is never placed into any [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] set; [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets only ever contain actual terminals (and possibly [latex]\$[/latex]).
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to Follow(S)": TRUE — this is the standard initialization rule, since nothing legitimately follows the start symbol except the end of input.

Answer: "ε is added to First(A) for A→ε" and "the end marker is added to Follow(S)" are both TRUE.

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text:
Consider a relational schema [latex] team(name, city, owner) [/latex], with functional dependencies [latex]\{ name \to city [/latex], [latex] name \to owner \} [/latex] .

The relation [latex] team [/latex] is decomposed into two relations, [latex] t_1(name, city) [/latex] and [latex] t_2(name, owner) [/latex]. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
options: (A) The relation [latex] team [/latex] is NOT in BCNF.
(B) The relations [latex] t_1 [/latex] and [latex] t_2 [/latex] are in BCNF.
(C) The decomposition constitutes a lossless join.
explanation:
[latex]team(name,city,owner)[/latex] with [latex]name\to city,\ name\to owner[/latex]. Since [latex]name[/latex] alone functionally determines every other attribute, [latex]name[/latex] is already a candidate key of [latex]team[/latex] — and since every FD's left-hand side ([latex]name[/latex]) is already a superkey, [latex]team[/latex] is already in BCNF (and hence also in 3NF) even before decomposing. So both "team is NOT in BCNF" and "team is NOT in 3NF" are false.

Decomposing into [latex]t_1(name,city)[/latex] and [latex]t_2(name,owner)[/latex]: in each projection, [latex]name[/latex] remains a key (it determines the sole remaining attribute), so both [latex]t_1[/latex] and [latex]t_2[/latex] are trivially in BCNF. True.

For losslessness, the common attribute of the decomposition is [latex]name[/latex], and [latex]name\to city[/latex] (i.e. [latex]name[/latex] alone determines all of [latex]t_1[/latex]) — satisfying the standard lossless-join test ([latex]R_1\cap R_2[/latex] is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces). True.

Answer: t1 and t2 are in BCNF; and the decomposition is lossless.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: "Everyone has exactly one mother"?

The meanings of the predicates used are:
[latex]mother(y,x): y[/latex] is the mother of [latex] x [/latex]
[latex]noteq(x,y): x[/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] are not equal
options: (A) [latex] \forall x \exists y \exists z (mother(y, x) \land \neg mother(z, x)) [/latex]
(B) [latex] \forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \forall z (noteq(z, y) \to \neg mother(z, x))] [/latex]
(C) [latex] \forall x \forall y [mother(y, x) \to \exists z (mother(z, x) \land \neg noteq(z, y))] [/latex]
(D) [latex] \forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \neg \exists z (noteq(z, y) \land mother(z, x))] [/latex]
explanation:
We want: for every person [latex]x[/latex], there is exactly one [latex]y[/latex] who is [latex]x[/latex]'s mother — meaning both existence (someone is the mother) and uniqueness (nobody else also qualifies as a distinct mother).

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))][/latex]: says "[latex]y[/latex] is a mother of [latex]x[/latex], and every [latex]z[/latex] different from [latex]y[/latex] is not a mother of [latex]x[/latex]" — this correctly captures existence plus uniqueness. Correct.

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))][/latex]: by De Morgan's law, [latex]\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))[/latex] is logically identical to [latex]\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))[/latex] — so this is just a different (but equivalent) way of writing the same correct statement above. Correct.

The other two options fail to properly express uniqueness: one only asserts some non-mother exists (too weak, says nothing about all other candidates), and the other is a vacuous implication that never actually forces a mother to exist at all.

Answer: Both the ∀x∃y[...∀z(noteq→¬mother)] form and its De Morgan-equivalent ∀x∃y[...¬∃z(noteq∧mother)] form are correct.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
[latex] A = \{ 0,1,2,3,\dots \} [/latex] is the set of non-negative integers. Let [latex] {F} [/latex] be the set of functions from [latex] A [/latex] to itself. For any two functions, [latex] f_1, f_2 \in {F} [/latex], we define

[latex] (f_1 \odot f_2)(n) = f_1(n) + f_2(n)[/latex]

for every number [latex] n [/latex] in [latex] A [/latex]. Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure [latex] ({F}, \odot ) [/latex]?
explanation:
[latex](f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)[/latex] — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers.

- Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so [latex]F[/latex] is closed under [latex]\odot[/latex].
- Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative.
- Identity: the constant-zero function [latex]z(n)=0[/latex] satisfies [latex]f\odot z=f[/latex] for every [latex]f[/latex] — an identity element exists.
- Commutativity: [latex]f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)[/latex] pointwise, so [latex]\odot[/latex] is commutative.
- Inverses: for a general [latex]f[/latex] (e.g. [latex]f(n)=n[/latex]), we'd need some [latex]g[/latex] with [latex]f(n)+g(n)=0[/latex], forcing [latex]g(n)=-f(n)[/latex] — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain [latex]A[/latex]. So inverses generally don't exist.

Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, [latex](F,\odot)[/latex] is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group).

Answer: (F, ⊙) is an Abelian monoid.

question_text: Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA) defined over the alphabet, [latex] \Sigma = \{ a, b \} [/latex]. Identify which of the following language(s) is/are accepted by the given DFA.
options: (A) The set of all strings containing an even number of [latex] b [/latex]'s.
(B) The set of all strings containing the pattern [latex] bab [/latex].
(C) The set of all strings ending with the pattern [latex] bab [/latex].
(D) The set of all strings not containing the pattern [latex] aba [/latex].
explanation:
This DFA, on inspection of its states and transitions, is built to track only the most recently seen [latex]3[/latex] input symbols, entering its unique accepting state precisely when those last three symbols read are exactly "[latex]bab[/latex]" — i.e. it's a standard "suffix detector" construction (a small sliding window of recent symbols, accepting whenever that window matches the target pattern at the very end of the input read so far).

This is a different (and stricter) condition than merely "contains bab somewhere" (that DFA would need to stay accepting once the pattern is seen, regardless of what comes after, rather than resetting/tracking only the tail) or "even number of b's" or "excludes aba" (which are entirely different acceptance conditions with different structural transitions).

Answer: The set of all strings ending with the pattern bab.

subject: Operating Systems
question_text: A disk of size [latex] 512M [/latex] bytes is divided into blocks of [latex] 64K [/latex] bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. Each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of [latex] 1M [/latex] bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, [latex] 1K=2^{10}, 1M=2^{20} [/latex]. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is _________. (Answer in integer)
explanation:
Disk block size [latex]=64K=2^{16}[/latex] bytes. In linked allocation, every block (including the last) reserves [latex]4[/latex] bytes for its "next" pointer field, leaving usable data capacity per block [latex]=65536-4=65532[/latex] bytes.

File size [latex]=1M=2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576[/latex] bytes. Number of blocks needed [latex]=\lceil1{,}048{,}576/65532\rceil[/latex]: since [latex]65532\times16=1{,}048{,}512[/latex] (short of the file size by [latex]64[/latex] bytes), a [latex]17[/latex]th block is required, giving [latex]17[/latex] blocks total.

Total disk space allocated [latex]=17\times65536=1{,}114{,}112[/latex] bytes. Space genuinely "useful" (actual file data plus the [latex]4[/latex]-byte pointer overhead in each of the [latex]17[/latex] blocks) [latex]=1{,}048{,}576+17\times4=1{,}048{,}576+68=1{,}048{,}644[/latex] bytes.

Internal fragmentation (wasted space) [latex]=1{,}114{,}112-1{,}048{,}644=65{,}468[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 65468

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is _________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
explanation:
This system uses hierarchical (serial) cache access: to reach L2, the processor must have already tried and missed in L1; to reach main memory, it must have already tried and missed in both L1 and L2. This means the given access-time figures for L2 and main memory already include the time already spent checking the earlier levels: L1 access time [latex]T_1=10[/latex] ns, L2 access time (which already includes the L1 miss penalty) [latex]T_2=20[/latex] ns, and main memory access time (already including both L1 and L2 miss penalties) [latex]T_3=200[/latex] ns. Hit rates: [latex]H_1=0.95[/latex] (L1), [latex]H_2=0.85[/latex] (L2).

The average memory access time is a weighted sum over the three possible outcomes — hit in L1, miss-L1-then-hit-L2, or miss-both-then-go-to-memory:
[latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)H_2T_2+(1-H_1)(1-H_2)T_3[/latex]
[latex]=0.95(10)+0.05(0.85)(20)+0.05(0.15)(200)[/latex]
[latex]=9.5+0.85+1.5=11.85[/latex] ns.

Answer: 11.85

question_text: Suppose a 5-bit message is transmitted from a source to a destination through a noisy channel. The probability that a bit of the message gets flipped during transmission is 0.01. question_text: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. question_text:
Consider a probability distribution given by the density function [latex] P(x) [/latex].

[latex] P(x) = \begin{cases} Cx^2, &\text{for } 1 \leq x \leq 4 \\ 0, & \text{for }x < 1 \text{ or } x > 4 \end{cases}[/latex]

[latex]C\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4=C\cdot\dfrac{64-1}{3}=21C=1\ \Rightarrow\ C=\dfrac1{21}[/latex]

[latex]P(2\le x\le3)=\displaystyle\int_2^3\dfrac{x^2}{21}\,dx=\dfrac1{21}\left[\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_2^3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{27-8}3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{19}3=\dfrac{19}{63}\approx0.302[/latex]

Answer: 0.302

So this group splits into [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex] and [latex]\{B,E\}[/latex].

For [latex]n=4[/latex] flip-flops, that's [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] states in the full cycle — i.e. [latex]7[/latex] other distinct states are visited before the circuit returns to repeat its initial state (with the full period being [latex]8[/latex] steps, depending on whether the initial state itself is counted in the tally).

Integrate by parts: with [latex]u=\ln t,\ dv=t\,dt[/latex] (so [latex]du=dt/t,\ v=t^2/2[/latex]):
[latex]\int t\ln t\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\int\dfrac{t}2\,dt=\dfrac{t^2}2\ln t-\dfrac{t^2}4[/latex]

Evaluating from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]x[/latex]: [latex]\left(\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4\right)-\left(0-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4+\dfrac14[/latex]

Setting this equal to [latex]\dfrac14[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4=0\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{x^2}2\left(\ln x-\dfrac12\right)=0[/latex]
Since [latex]x>1[/latex] means [latex]x^2\ne0[/latex], we need [latex]\ln x=\dfrac12\ \Rightarrow\ x=e^{1/2}=\sqrt e[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\sqrt{e}[/latex]

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text:
Consider a binary tree [latex]T [/latex] in which every node has either zero or two children. Let [latex]n > 0 [/latex] be the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex].
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in [latex]T [/latex] that have exactly two children?
explanation:
In a binary tree where every node has [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children, let [latex]I[/latex] be the number of [latex]2[/latex]-children (internal) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] the number of leaves. A basic counting fact for such trees: [latex]L=I+1[/latex] (each internal node, when added, net-increases the leaf count by exactly one over what it replaced).

Total nodes: [latex]n=I+L=I+(I+1)=2I+1\ \Rightarrow\ I=\dfrac{n-1}2[/latex]

Answer: (n-1)/2

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question_text:
Let [latex]L [/latex], [latex]M [/latex], and [latex]N [/latex] be non-singular matrices of order 3 satisfying the equations

[latex] L^2 = L^{-1}, \quad M = L^8, \quad N = L^2. [/latex]

Which ONE of the following is the value of the determinant of [latex](M - N) [/latex]?
explanation:
From [latex]L^2=L^{-1}[/latex], multiply both sides by [latex]L[/latex]: [latex]L^3=L^2\cdot L=L^{-1}\cdot L=I[/latex]. So [latex]L[/latex] has order dividing [latex]3[/latex].

[latex]M=L^8=L^{6+2}=(L^3)^2\cdot L^2=I^2\cdot L^2=L^2[/latex]. But we're also given [latex]N=L^2[/latex]. So [latex]M=N[/latex] exactly, meaning [latex]M-N[/latex] is the zero matrix.

[latex]\det(M-N)=\det(0)=0[/latex]

Answer: 0

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text: Let [latex]P(x) [/latex] be an arbitrary predicate over the domain of natural numbers. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
explanation:
This is exactly the statement of the principle of mathematical induction: if a predicate [latex]P[/latex] holds for the base case [latex]0[/latex], and truth of [latex]P(x)[/latex] always guarantees truth of [latex]P(x+1)[/latex] (the inductive step, moving forward), then [latex]P[/latex] holds for every natural number.

The other options either use a backward step ([latex]P(x)\Rightarrow P(x-1)[/latex], which can't reach numbers larger than the base case) or start from a base case like [latex]1000[/latex] (which, even with a valid forward or backward step, can never establish [latex]P[/latex] for numbers below [latex]1000[/latex] using only a one-directional step) — none of these actually guarantee [latex]P[/latex] for every natural number.

Answer: (P(0) ∧ (∀x[P(x)⇒P(x+1)])) ⇒ (∀x P(x))

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
Consider the following statements:

(i) Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
(ii) A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgement for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?
explanation:
(i) ARP maps IP addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses: this is exactly ARP's definition — TRUE.

(ii) "A single TCP segment cannot carry both data and an acknowledgement": this is FALSE. TCP is full-duplex, and a very common optimization called piggybacking lets a single outgoing segment simultaneously carry new data (from S to R) and an acknowledgement field (ACKing previously received data from R) — the TCP header always has an ACK field available regardless of whether the segment also carries data.

Answer: (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
Consider the routing protocols given in List I and the names given in List II:

[latex]\begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Distance vector routing} & \text{(a)} & \text{Bellman-Ford} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Link state routing} & \text{(b)} & \text{Dijkstra} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
explanation:
Distance vector routing is the practical, distributed implementation of the Bellman-Ford shortest-path algorithm (each router only knows next-hop distances from its neighbors, iteratively). Link state routing requires full topology knowledge at each router and computes shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm.

Answer: (i)-(a) and (ii)-(b)

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.
Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?
explanation:
The IPv4 protocol field identifies which higher-layer protocol's data the datagram carries, using standard registered numbers: ICMP [latex]=1[/latex], IGMP [latex]=2[/latex], OSPF [latex]=89[/latex] — all of these run directly over IP and have their own dedicated protocol number.

RIP, however, is not carried directly over IP; it runs as an application-layer protocol on top of UDP (using UDP port [latex]520[/latex]). So an IP datagram carrying RIP traffic would have its protocol field set to UDP's number ([latex]17[/latex]), never a dedicated "RIP" protocol number.

Answer: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

subject: Programming and Data Structures
explanation:
[latex]a="@\#Hello\ World!"[/latex] occupies indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]14[/latex] (`@`,`#`,`H`,`e`,`l`,`l`,`o`,` `,`W`,`o`,`r`,`l`,`d`,`!`,`\0`). [latex]\text{stringcopy(a, a+2)}[/latex] sets [latex]s=a[/latex] (index [latex]0[/latex]) and [latex]t=a+2[/latex] (index [latex]2[/latex]), copying forward while [latex]{*}t[/latex] is non-null (checked before each copy).

Since the loop condition is checked before copying, it copies indices [latex]2[/latex] through [latex]13[/latex] (`H` through `!`, [latex]12[/latex] characters) into destination indices [latex]0[/latex] through [latex]11[/latex], then stops as soon as [latex]{*}t[/latex] hits the original null at index [latex]14[/latex] — without ever writing a new null terminator into the destination.

So after the copy: indices [latex]0[/latex]-[latex]11[/latex] hold the shifted text `Hello World!`, but indices [latex]12,13,14[/latex] still hold their original, untouched values: `d`, `!`, and the original `\0`.

[latex]\text{printf("\%s")}[/latex] prints from index [latex]0[/latex] until it hits the first null — which is still the original one at index [latex]14[/latex]. So it prints: `Hello World!` (indices 0-11) followed by the leftover `d` (index 12) and `!` (index 13) before finally stopping at the null.

Answer: Hello World!d!

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text:
Consider an unordered list of [latex]N [/latex] distinct integers.
What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?
explanation:
We just need to find some element guaranteed not to be the overall largest — not identify the largest itself, and not verify anything about the rest of the list.

Compare any two elements of the list against each other: whichever of the two is smaller is guaranteed to not be the maximum of the whole list (since the larger of this pair beats it, so it can't possibly be the overall largest). This requires only one comparison, and works for any list of [latex]N\ge2[/latex] distinct integers.

Answer: 1

subject: Compiler Design
question_text:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation:

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.
(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
explanation:
(I) Backpatching for Boolean expressions in one pass: TRUE — this is exactly backpatching's classic use case: jump targets for [latex]\text{true}[/latex]/[latex]\text{false}[/latex] lists are left unfilled initially and "patched in" once the actual target address becomes known later, avoiding the need for a second pass.

(II) Backpatching for flow-of-control statements (if/while) in one pass: also TRUE — the same technique is used to generate code for conditional and looping constructs single-pass, patching jump instructions once the relevant labels are determined.

Answer: Both (I) and (II) are correct.

subject: Compiler Design
question_text:
Given the following syntax-directed translation rules:

[latex] \text{Rule 1: } R \rightarrow AB \{ B.i = R.i - 1; A.i = B.i; R.i = A.i + 1; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 2: } P \rightarrow CD \{ P.i = C.i + D.i; D.i = C.i + 2; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 3: } Q \rightarrow EF \{ Q.i = E.i + F.i; \} [/latex]

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?
options: (A) Rule 1 is S-attributed and L-attributed;  Rule 2 is S-attributed and not L-attributed;  Rule 3 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.
(B) Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
(C) Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
(D) Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
explanation:
Classify each rule by whether it uses only synthesized attributes (S-attributed: every attribute is computed purely from children) versus whether it's L-attributed (inherited attributes may only depend on the parent or strictly-left siblings, evaluated left to right):

Rule 1 ([latex]R\to AB\{B.i=R.i-1;\ A.i=B.i;\ R.i=A.i+1;\}[/latex]): [latex]A.i[/latex] is defined using [latex]B.i[/latex] — but [latex]B[/latex] is to the right of [latex]A[/latex] in the production, so this inherited-attribute dependency flows backward (right-to-left), violating L-attributed rules. It's also not S-attributed, since [latex]B.i[/latex] is set from [latex]R.i[/latex] (an inherited attribute from the parent). Neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.

Rule 2 ([latex]P\to CD\{P.i=C.i+D.i;\ D.i=C.i+2;\}[/latex]): [latex]D.i[/latex] (inherited) is set using only [latex]C.i[/latex], a left sibling — perfectly valid for L-attributed. But since [latex]D[/latex] does have an inherited attribute at all, the SDT is not purely synthesized. Not S-attributed, but is L-attributed.

Rule 3 ([latex]Q\to EF\{Q.i=E.i+F.i;\}[/latex]): the only attribute defined is [latex]Q.i[/latex], computed purely from its children [latex]E,F[/latex] — purely synthesized. S-attributed (and therefore also L-attributed, since S-attributed is a special case of L-attributed).

Answer: Rule 1 is neither; Rule 2 is not S-attributed but is L-attributed; Rule 3 is both S-attributed and L-attributed.

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
explanation:
Ethernet frame data field max [latex]=1500[/latex] bytes; IPv4 header [latex]=20[/latex] bytes (no options), so max IP data per fragment [latex]=1500-20=1480[/latex] bytes — conveniently already a multiple of [latex]8[/latex], so no further rounding needed.

The UDP segment (header [latex]8[/latex] bytes [latex]+[/latex] payload [latex]7488[/latex] bytes [latex]=7496[/latex] bytes) becomes the IP datagram's data, which must be fragmented:
[latex]7496\div1480=5.06\ldots[/latex], so [latex]5[/latex] full fragments of [latex]1480[/latex] bytes ([latex]7400[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]7496-7400=96[/latex] bytes of data.

Total fragments [latex]=5+1=6[/latex]. Last fragment's total size (including its own [latex]20[/latex]-byte IP header) [latex]=96+20=116[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 6 fragments, 116 bytes

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?
options: (C) Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.
explanation:
A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs), which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA.

Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA.

"Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable.

Answer: Any regular language.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Let [latex]G_1, G_2 [/latex] be Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) and [latex]R [/latex] be a regular expression. For a grammar [latex]G [/latex], let [latex]L(G) [/latex] denote the language generated by [latex]G [/latex].
Which ONE among the following questions is decidable?
explanation:
Checking the decidability of each question about context-free grammars:

- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(G_2)[/latex]? Undecidable — equivalence of two context-free grammars is a classic undecidable problem.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)\cap L(G_2)=\emptyset[/latex]? Undecidable — intersection-emptiness of two CFLs is undecidable (context-free languages aren't even closed under intersection in general, and this question is known to be undecidable, related to the Post Correspondence Problem).
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=L(R)[/latex]? (comparing a CFG's language to a regular language) Undecidable in general — this is essentially as hard as general CFG equivalence, since a regular language is just a special case of a context-free one.
- Is [latex]L(G_1)=\emptyset[/latex]? Decidable! Emptiness of a single CFG's language can be checked with a simple, standard algorithm: iteratively mark which non-terminals can derive some terminal string, starting from productions with only terminals, and propagating upward — the language is empty iff the start symbol never gets marked.

Answer: Is L(G1) = ∅? (this is the only decidable one)

subject: Operating Systems
topic: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority)
question_text:
Processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 [/latex] arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.
Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?
explanation:
Simulate SRTF (always run whichever available process has the least remaining time):

[latex]t{=}0[/latex]: only [latex]P_1[/latex] present (remaining [latex]10[/latex]) → runs.
[latex]t{=}1[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]13[/latex]); [latex]P_1[/latex]'s remaining ([latex]9[/latex]) is still shortest → [latex]P_1[/latex] continues.
[latex]t{=}2[/latex]: [latex]P_3[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]6[/latex]); now shortest among [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_3[/latex]([latex]6[/latex]) is [latex]P_3[/latex] → switch to [latex]P_3[/latex].
[latex]P_3[/latex] runs uninterrupted [latex]t{=}2[/latex] to [latex]t{=}8[/latex] (no shorter arrivals in between), finishing exactly as [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives. [latex]P_3[/latex] turnaround [latex]=8-2=6[/latex].
[latex]t{=}8[/latex]: [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]9[/latex]); comparing [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_1[/latex] shortest, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}16[/latex]. [latex]P_1[/latex] turnaround [latex]=16-0=16[/latex].
[latex]t{=}16[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]) vs [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_4[/latex] runs to completion at [latex]t{=}25[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=25-8=17[/latex].
[latex]t{=}25[/latex]: only [latex]P_2[/latex] left, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}38[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=38-1=37[/latex].

Average turnaround [latex]=\dfrac{6+16+17+37}4=\dfrac{76}4=19[/latex]

Answer: 19

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account [latex]A [/latex] attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account [latex]A [/latex] to account [latex]B [/latex]. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in [latex]A [/latex] and were allowed to go through. [latex]B [/latex] was credited Rs. 10000 twice. [latex]A [/latex] was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.
Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
explanation:
This is a classic lost-update anomaly caused by two transactions reading the same stale value and overwriting each other's effects.

- Consistency is violated: the database ends up in a state that breaks the intended invariant (money should be conserved / correctly transferred), since [latex]A[/latex] should have ended up [latex]11000-20000[/latex] worth adjusted correctly but instead only one debit actually applied while both credits landed — the books don't balance as intended.
- Isolation is violated: the two concurrent transactions were not properly isolated from each other — both read [latex]A[/latex]'s balance before either had committed its update, letting their effects clash (textbook lost-update problem).
- Atomicity is not necessarily violated: each individual transaction ran to completion in full (no partial execution of a single transaction occurred).
- Durability is unrelated here: there's no indication of any committed-then-lost data due to a crash.

Answer: Consistency and Isolation

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
options: (A) The size of the cache memory
(B) The clock frequency of the processor
(C) The number of cache memory levels
explanation:
The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the software-visible contract between hardware and software — things like available instructions, addressing modes, and the visible register set. The total number of (architecturally visible) registers is part of this contract, since programs/compilers must know how many registers they can target.

Cache size, clock frequency, and number of cache levels are all microarchitecture (implementation) details — two processors implementing the very same ISA can freely differ in these without breaking software compatibility.

Answer: The total number of registers

subject: Algorithms
question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?
options: (A) A DFS tree of [latex]G [/latex] is a Shortest Path tree of [latex]G [/latex].
(B) Every non-tree edge of [latex]G [/latex] with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.

(C) If [latex](u, v) [/latex] is a non-tree edge of [latex]G [/latex] with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex [latex]s [/latex] to [latex]u [/latex] and [latex]v [/latex] in the BFS tree are within [latex]\pm 1 [/latex] of each other.
(D) Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of [latex]G [/latex].
explanation:
Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph:

- "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that.
- "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge": true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back).
- "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1": true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels.
- "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components": true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components.

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th statements are all true.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c l|c l|} \hline \textbf{List I} & & \textbf{List II} & \\ \hline \text{(i)} & \text{Context free languages} & \text{(a)} & \text{Closed under union} \\ \hline \text{(ii)} & \text{Recursive languages} & \text{(b)} & \text{Not closed under complementation} \\ \hline \text{(iii)} & \text{Regular languages} & \text{(c)} & \text{Closed under intersection} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
explanation:
Recall the closure properties: Context-free languages are closed under union, but famously not closed under complementation (matching (i)-(b)) and also not closed under intersection in general. Recursive languages and regular languages are each closed under both union and intersection (both (a) and (c) hold true for each of them) — so either valid assignment of (a)/(c) across (ii) and (iii) gives a fully correct matching, as long as (i) is paired with (b) (the one property that specifically distinguishes CFLs from the other two classes).

This is exactly why two different complete matchings both check out as correct: (i)-(b), (ii)-(a), (iii)-(c) and (i)-(b), (ii)-(c), (iii)-(a) — since recursive and regular languages don't care which of (a)/(c) is assigned to which, both being true of both.

Answer: (i)-(b),(ii)-(a),(iii)-(c) AND (i)-(b),(ii)-(c),(iii)-(a)

subject: Digital Logic
question_text:
Consider the following logic circuit diagram.

Which is/are the CORRECT option(s) for the output function [latex]F [/latex]?
explanation:
From the given circuit: a NAND gate takes inputs [latex]X,Y[/latex] directly, giving [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; a separate inverter taps the [latex]X[/latex] line alone, giving [latex]\bar X[/latex]; and a third branch inverts [latex]Y[/latex] then ANDs it with [latex]X[/latex], giving [latex]X\bar Y[/latex]. All three signals feed into a final OR gate:

[latex]F=\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex]

By De Morgan's law, [latex]\overline{XY}=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex], so this simplifies to [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]. But the term [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is already fully covered/absorbed by [latex]\bar Y[/latex] alone (whenever [latex]X\bar Y[/latex] is true, [latex]\bar Y[/latex] is automatically true too) — so by the absorption law, [latex]F=\bar X+\bar Y[/latex] exactly, which is the same function as [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex] itself.

So [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex], [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex], and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] are all just different (redundant) ways of writing the exact same underlying function; only [latex]X+\bar Y[/latex] is a genuinely different function.

Answer: [latex]\overline{XY}[/latex]; [latex]\bar X+\bar Y+X\bar Y[/latex]; and [latex]\overline{XY}+\bar X+X\bar Y[/latex] (all equivalent, all correct).

subject: Digital Logic
question_text:
The following two signed 2's complement numbers (multiplicand [latex]M [/latex] and multiplier [latex]Q [/latex]) are being multiplied using Booth's algorithm:

[latex] M: 1100 \, 1101 \, 1110 \, 1101 \quad \text{and} \quad Q: 1010 \, 0100 \, 1010 \, 1010 [/latex]

The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is ________. (Answer in integer)
explanation:
In Booth's algorithm, an addition or subtraction is performed at every bit-position where the pair (current [latex]Q_0[/latex] bit, previous bit [latex]Q_{-1}[/latex], initialized to [latex]0[/latex]) shows a transition ("01" → add [latex]M[/latex], "10" → subtract [latex]M[/latex]); a run of identical bits ("00" or "11") triggers no arithmetic operation, just a shift.

Scanning [latex]Q=1010\,0100\,1010\,1010[/latex] (appended with the initial [latex]Q_{-1}=0[/latex]) for every "01" or "10" transition between consecutive bit pairs gives [latex]13[/latex] such transition points out of the [latex]16[/latex] total bit-positions.

subject: Digital Logic
question_text: In a 4-bit ripple counter, if the period of the waveform at the last flip-flop is 64 microseconds, then the frequency of the ripple counter in kHz is ________. (Answer in integer)
explanation:
In an [latex]n[/latex]-bit ripple counter, each successive flip-flop's output has exactly half the frequency (double the period) of the one before it, since each stage divides the input clock frequency by [latex]2[/latex]. The last (4th) flip-flop's period is therefore [latex]2^4=16[/latex] times the input clock's period.

Input clock period [latex]=\dfrac{64\ \mu s}{16}=4\ \mu s[/latex], so input clock frequency [latex]=\dfrac1{4\ \mu s}=250{,}000[/latex] Hz [latex]=250[/latex] kHz.

Answer: 250

question_text:
Suppose we are transmitting frames between two nodes using the Stop-and-Wait protocol. The frame size is 3000 bits. The transmission rate of the channel is 2000 bps (bits/second) and the propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds. Assume that the processing times at the source and destination are negligible. Also, assume that the size of the acknowledgment packet is negligible.  
Which ONE of the following most accurately gives the channel utilization for the above scenario in percentage?
explanation:
Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{3000\text{ bits}}{2000\text{ bps}}=1.5[/latex] s. Propagation delay [latex]T_p=0.1[/latex] s (one-way).

In Stop-and-Wait, the sender must wait a full round trip (plus negligible ack transmission/processing time) after sending each frame before sending the next:
Utilization [latex]=\dfrac{T_t}{T_t+2T_p}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.5+0.2}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.7}\approx0.8823=88.23\%[/latex]
