subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] be defined as follows:

[latex] f(x)=\left(\frac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\frac{|x|}{2}\right) [/latex]

Which of the following statements is/are true?
explanation:
Simplify [latex]f(x)=\left(\dfrac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)=-\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)^2[/latex], which is always [latex]\le0[/latex].

- For [latex]x\ge0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{x^2}{4}[/latex].
- For [latex]x<0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=-x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{9x^2}{4}[/latex].

Both pieces equal [latex]0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] and are negative (and decreasing towards [latex]-\infty[/latex]) moving away from [latex]0[/latex] in either direction. So [latex]f[/latex] has a clear local (in fact global) maximum at [latex]x=0[/latex], and since [latex]f\to-\infty[/latex] on both sides with no interior dip, [latex]f[/latex] has no local minimum.

[latex]f'(x)=-x/2[/latex] for [latex]x\ge0[/latex] and [latex]f'(x)=-9x/2[/latex] for [latex]x<0[/latex]. Both pieces approach [latex]0[/latex] as [latex]x\to0[/latex], so [latex]f'[/latex] is continuous everywhere including at [latex]0[/latex]. But the slope of [latex]f'[/latex] jumps from [latex]-1/2[/latex] (just right of [latex]0[/latex]) to [latex]-9/2[/latex] (just left of [latex]0[/latex]), so [latex]f'[/latex] has a corner at [latex]x=0[/latex] and is not differentiable there (hence not differentiable "over [latex]\mathbb R[/latex]").

Answer: f has a local maximum; f' is continuous over R; f' is not differentiable over R.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected graph. A vertex cover of [latex]G[/latex] is a subset [latex]V^{\prime} \subseteq V[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, u \in V^{\prime}[/latex] or [latex]v \in V^{\prime}[/latex]. Let the size of the smallest vertex cover in [latex]G[/latex] be [latex]k[/latex]. Let [latex]S[/latex] be any vertex cover of size [latex]k[/latex].

For a vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], which of the following constraints will always ensure that [latex]v \in S[/latex] ?
options: (A) The degree of [latex]v[/latex] is at least [latex]k+1[/latex]
(B) The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a path of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
(C) The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a cycle of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
(D) The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is a part of a clique of size [latex]k[/latex]
explanation:
Suppose, for contradiction, [latex]v[/latex] has degree [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] but [latex]v\notin S[/latex] for some minimum vertex cover [latex]S[/latex] of size [latex]k[/latex]. Since [latex]v\notin S[/latex], every edge incident on [latex]v[/latex] must be covered by its other endpoint (because [latex]S[/latex] is a vertex cover), so all [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] distinct neighbors of [latex]v[/latex] must belong to [latex]S[/latex]. But then [latex]|S|\ge k+1>k[/latex], contradicting that [latex]S[/latex] has size exactly [latex]k[/latex]. So [latex]v[/latex] must be in every minimum vertex cover.

The other conditions don't force inclusion: a vertex on a long path or cycle can often be excluded by choosing the cover among its neighbors instead; and being part of a size-[latex]k[/latex] clique only forces [latex]k-1[/latex] of the clique's vertices into the cover (any one clique vertex, including [latex]v[/latex], can be the one left out).

Answer: "The degree of v is at least k+1" always forces v ∈ S.

subject: Digital Logic
question_text:
Consider a Boolean function [latex]F[/latex] with the following minterm expression:

[latex] F(P, Q, R, S)=\sum m(1,2,3,4,5,7,10,12,13,14) [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are the minimal sum-of-products expression(s) of [latex]F[/latex] ?
explanation:
Plotting [latex]F(P,Q,R,S)=\sum m(1,2,3,4,5,7,10,12,13,14)[/latex] on a [latex]4[/latex]-variable K-map, the essential prime implicants are [latex]\bar P S[/latex] (covering minterms [latex]1,3,5,7[/latex]) and [latex]Q\bar R[/latex] (covering [latex]4,5,12,13[/latex]).

After these two terms, the still-uncovered minterms are [latex]2,10,14[/latex] (minterm [latex]3,4,5,12,13[/latex] already covered). These three remaining minterms can be covered in two equally minimal ways, giving two different valid minimal SOP expressions:

- Using [latex]\bar P\bar Q R[/latex] (covers [latex]2,3[/latex]) and [latex]P R\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]10,14[/latex]): [latex]F=\bar P S+Q\bar R+\bar P\bar Q R+PR\bar S[/latex].
- Using [latex]PQ\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]12,14[/latex]) and [latex]\bar Q R\bar S[/latex] (covers [latex]2,10[/latex]): [latex]F=\bar P S+Q\bar R+PQ\bar S+\bar Q R\bar S[/latex].

Both use exactly [latex]4[/latex] terms and correctly cover all [latex]10[/latex] minterms with none extra, so both are valid minimal-cost solutions (this function has two equally-good minimal SOP forms because the remaining minterms admit two different but equally cheap coverings).

Answer: [latex]\bar P S+Q\bar R+\bar P\bar Q R+PR\bar S[/latex] and [latex]\bar P S+Q\bar R+PQ\bar S+\bar Q R\bar S[/latex]

subject: Algorithms
question_text: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of [latex]G[/latex] is/are true?
options: (A) In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the largest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is not in any MST
(B) In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is in every MST
(C) For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the largest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is not in any MST
(D) For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is in every MST
explanation:
When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique, and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply:

- Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True.
- The claim about the smallest-weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping).
- The claim that the largest-weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph.
- Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True.

Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST.

subject: Algorithms
question_text:
Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] as input, where [latex]d[v][/latex] and [latex]f[v][/latex] are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex]. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \begin{array}{l} \textbf{DFS}(G): \\ \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): \\ \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Suppose that the input directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
explanation:
For a DAG, discovery/finish-time intervals [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] obtained from DFS obey the standard parenthesis theorem: for any two vertices, their intervals are either completely nested (one inside the other) or completely disjoint — they can never partially overlap.

For an edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] in a DAG, DFS classifies it as either a tree/forward edge (if [latex]v[/latex] is discovered while exploring from [latex]u[/latex], nesting [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] inside [latex][d[u],f[u]][/latex], giving [latex]d[u]cross edge (if [latex]v[/latex] was already fully explored before [latex]u[/latex] started, giving disjoint, non-overlapping intervals [latex]d[v]
- [latex]d[u] - [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[v]back edge — impossible in a DAG.
- [latex]d[u]never happen for any DFS on any graph, regardless of edge type.

Answer: [latex]d[v]

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Let [latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] be two languages over a finite alphabet, such that [latex]L_{1} \cap L_{2}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are regular languages.
Which of the following statements is/are always true?
explanation:
Given: [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex] is regular, and [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular.

- [latex]L_1[/latex] regular? Not necessarily — [latex]L_1[/latex] could be an arbitrary (even non-context-free) language whose intersection with a specific regular [latex]L_2[/latex] happens to simplify to something regular; this doesn't pin down [latex]L_1[/latex] itself. Not always true.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex] regular? Same issue — the union still depends on the unconstrained, potentially irregular parts of [latex]L_1[/latex] outside of [latex]L_2[/latex]. Not always true.
- [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] context-free? Since [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular, its complement [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is also regular (regular languages are closed under complement), and every regular language is also context-free (regular [latex]\subset[/latex] context-free). Always true.
- [latex]L_1[/latex] context-free? No general closure property forces this; [latex]L_1[/latex] could even be undecidable/non-context-free as long as it agrees with [latex]L_2[/latex] on the intersection. Not always true.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is context-free.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a b a A B A b b a \\ A \rightarrow a a B B A b \mid b B a b a a \\ B \rightarrow a B b \mid a b \end{array} [/latex]

In the above grammar, [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols, and [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are non-terminal symbols.

Let [latex]L(G)[/latex] be the language generated by the grammar [latex]G[/latex]. For a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex], let [latex]n_{1}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]a[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex] and [latex]n_{2}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]b[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: (A) There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s) < n_{2}(s)[/latex]
(B) For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \geq n_{2}(s)[/latex]
(C) There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s)>2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]
(D) For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \leq 2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]
explanation:
[latex]B\rightarrow aBb\mid ab[/latex] always generates strings of the form [latex]a^kb^k[/latex] ([latex]k\ge1[/latex]) — equal numbers of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, i.e. [latex]n_1=n_2[/latex] within any string derived from [latex]B[/latex].

[latex]A\rightarrow aaBBAb\mid bBabaa[/latex]: substituting the fact that each [latex]B[/latex]-string contributes equal [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, and tracking the extra fixed terminals in each production, one can verify by induction that every string derivable from [latex]A[/latex] satisfies [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] (the fixed terminal parts always contribute at least as many, often more, [latex]a[/latex]'s as [latex]b[/latex]'s on top of the balanced [latex]B[/latex]-parts), and also that [latex]n_1(s)\le 2\,n_2(s)[/latex] always (the excess of [latex]a[/latex]'s over [latex]b[/latex]'s is bounded relative to the total [latex]b[/latex] count, because of the specific fixed ratio of terminals baked into each production).

[latex]S\rightarrow abaABAbba[/latex] adds a further fixed collection of terminals ([latex]4[/latex] [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]4[/latex] [latex]b[/latex]'s from the frame, plus two copies of an [latex]A[/latex]-string), and this fixed frame preserves the same two invariants that hold for [latex]A[/latex]: every generated string has [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] and [latex]n_1(s)\le2\,n_2(s)[/latex], with no derivable string ever violating either bound.

Answer: For every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex]; and for every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\le2n_2(s)[/latex].

subject: Compiler Design
question_text:
Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions [latex]\text{SDD1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{SDD2}[/latex] for type declarations.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD1}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_1) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow TV & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ V.type = T.type \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} V_1.type = V.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline V \rightarrow \text{id} & \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD2}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_2) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow D_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = D_1.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, }D_1.type) \end{array} \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, T.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex]D[/latex] is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal [latex]V_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]V[/latex] and the non-terminal [latex]D_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]D[/latex]. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier.

Let [latex]\text{P}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] be the languages specified by grammars [latex]\text{G1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{G2}[/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: (A) The languages P and Q are the same
(B) SSD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
(C) SSD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
(D) The specifications of SSD1 and SSD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table
explanation:
Language equivalence: [latex]G_1[/latex] generates a type keyword followed by one-or-more identifiers (via the recursive [latex]V[/latex]); [latex]G_2[/latex] generates the same thing via a left-recursive [latex]D[/latex]. Both accept exactly "type-keyword followed by [latex]\ge1[/latex] identifiers," so [latex]P=Q[/latex]. True.

SDD2's attribute style: In SDD2, [latex]D.type[/latex] and the [latex]\text{put}[/latex] actions are all computed purely from the values of the symbols on the right-hand side of each production (children of the node in the parse tree) — every attribute is synthesized, making SDD2 S-attributed. True.

SDD1's attribute style: In SDD1, [latex]V.type[/latex] is set from [latex]T.type[/latex] (an inherited value flowing top-down from the parent [latex]D[/latex] into [latex]V[/latex], then further down into [latex]V_1[/latex]), so SDD1 does use inherited attributes — but [latex]D.type[/latex] itself is synthesized from [latex]T.type[/latex] as well, so SDD1 is L-attributed but it is not true that it contains "only" inherited attributes (it has both kinds). False as stated.

Symbol table contents: In SDD1, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, V.type)}[/latex] is called for every identifier with the type inherited down from [latex]T[/latex]. In SDD2, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, ...type)}[/latex] is similarly called for every identifier with the same type value (synthesized bottom-up instead, but numerically identical since there's only one [latex]T[/latex]/type per declaration). Since both add exactly one entry per identifier with the same type value, the symbol tables end up identical. True.

Answer: P and Q are the same language; SDD2 is S-attributed with only synthesized attributes; and both SDDs populate the symbol table with the same entries.

subject: Operating Systems
question_text:
Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid.

For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?
options: (A) TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit
(B) TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit
(C) TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit
(D) TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss
explanation:
A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache.

- TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen.
- TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page.
- TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible.
- TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident.

Answer: "TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit" and "TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit" can NEVER happen.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is said to be [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if there exists a function [latex]c: V \rightarrow\{0,1\}[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, c(u) \neq c(v)[/latex].

Which of the following statements about [latex]2[/latex]-colorable graphs is/are true?
options: (A) If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of odd length
(B) If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of even length
(C) An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list
(D) An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|E| \log |V|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list
explanation:
A graph is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if and only if it is bipartite, which is exactly equivalent to having no odd-length cycle.

- "May contain cycles of odd length" — false, a 2-colorable graph can never contain an odd cycle (that's precisely the bipartiteness characterization).
- "May contain cycles of even length" — true, even cycles are perfectly fine in a bipartite graph (e.g. alternating the two colors around the cycle works exactly when the cycle length is even).
- Algorithm complexity: Testing bipartiteness/[latex]2[/latex]-colorability is done via a single BFS or DFS traversal, alternately coloring each vertex as it's visited and checking for conflicts — this runs in [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex] time on an adjacency-list representation, and this is optimal since you must at least look at every vertex and edge once. True.
- [latex]\Theta(|E|\log|V|)[/latex] is not the optimal/typical complexity for this simple traversal-based check (that bound is more associated with, e.g., priority-queue-based MST/shortest-path algorithms), so this is false as a claim about the optimal algorithm for 2-colorability testing.

Answer: G may contain even-length cycles; and the optimal 2-colorability test runs in Θ(|V|+|E|) time.

subject: Computer Networks
question_text: An ISP having an address block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] assigns a block of [latex]6000[/latex] IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
explanation:
The ISP's block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] spans two full class-B-sized blocks: all addresses from [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex] to [latex]202.17.255.255[/latex].

For [latex]6000[/latex] addresses via CIDR super-netting, we need a block with at least [latex]6000[/latex] addresses; a [latex]/19[/latex] prefix gives [latex]2^{32-19}=2^{13}=8192[/latex] addresses, which suffices (a [latex]/20[/latex] would only give [latex]4096<6000[/latex]).

A valid [latex]/19[/latex] sub-block must (a) lie entirely within [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex]-[latex]202.17.255.255[/latex], and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] in the relevant octet (since [latex]/19[/latex] leaves [latex]13[/latex] host bits, and [latex]2^{13}=8192=32\times256[/latex] addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of [latex]32[/latex]: [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]).

- [latex]202.16.0.0/19[/latex]: [latex]0[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], and within range. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.64.0/19[/latex]: [latex]64[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], [latex]202.17.x[/latex] is within the /15 range. Valid.
- [latex]202.16.32.0/19[/latex]: [latex]32[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex]. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.24.0/19[/latex]: [latex]24[/latex] is not a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] (valid boundaries are [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]), so this is not a properly aligned [latex]/19[/latex] block. Invalid.

Answer: 202.16.0.0/19, 202.17.64.0/19, and 202.16.32.0/19 can be assigned.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected graph, which is a path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices. The number of matchings in [latex]G[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation:
Let [latex]f(k)[/latex] denote the number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with [latex]k[/latex] edges. Considering the last edge of the path: either it is not used in the matching (leaving [latex]f(k-1)[/latex] choices for the rest), or it is used (which forbids the adjacent edge, leaving [latex]f(k-2)[/latex] choices for the rest). This gives the Fibonacci-like recurrence:
[latex]f(k)=f(k-1)+f(k-2)[/latex], with [latex]f(0)=1[/latex] (no edges: only the empty matching) and [latex]f(1)=2[/latex] (one edge: either included or not).

[latex]f(2)=3,\ f(3)=5,\ f(4)=8,\ f(5)=13,\ f(6)=21,\ f(7)=34[/latex].

A path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices has [latex]7[/latex] edges, so the number of matchings is [latex]f(7)=34[/latex].

Answer: 34

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of [latex]15000[/latex] rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Initially, the head is on track [latex]0[/latex]. The number of sectors per track is [latex]400[/latex]. The sector size is [latex]1024[/latex] bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from [latex]10[/latex] randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: [latex]5, 12[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex].

The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation:
Rotation time per revolution [latex]=\dfrac{60000\text{ ms}}{15000}=4[/latex] ms, so average rotational latency (half a revolution) [latex]=2[/latex] ms, and time per sector [latex]=\dfrac{4\text{ ms}}{400\text{ sectors}}=0.01[/latex] ms.

Seek time (head moves [latex]1[/latex] ms per adjacent track, following the path [latex]0\to5\to12\to7[/latex]):
[latex]0\to5[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms; [latex]5\to12[/latex]: [latex]7[/latex] tracks [latex]=7[/latex] ms; [latex]12\to7[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms. Total seek [latex]=5+7+5=17[/latex] ms.

Data transfer per track: since the [latex]10[/latex] sectors needed are randomly located, each individual sector access requires (on average) a fresh rotational latency of [latex]2[/latex] ms before the required sector arrives under the head, plus the [latex]0.01[/latex] ms to actually read it:
Per track [latex]=10\times(2+0.01)=20.1[/latex] ms. Over [latex]3[/latex] tracks: [latex]3\times20.1=60.3[/latex] ms.

Total time [latex]=[/latex] seek [latex]+[/latex] transfer [latex]=17+60.3=77.3[/latex] ms.

Answer: 77.3

question_text:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] and [latex]M[/latex] (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of [latex]100[/latex] instructions for a program P ), are given in the table below.

The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is [latex]1[/latex] nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|} \hline \text{Instruction} & \begin{array}{c} t_{EX}\ \text{in} \\ \text{nanoseconds} \end{array} & M \\ \hline \text{LOAD} & 1.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{IMUL} & 1.5 & 10 \\ \hline \text{IDIV} & 2.5 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FADD} & 1.7 & 10 \\ \hline \text{FSUB} & 1.7 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FMUL} & 2.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{FDIV} & 3.2 & 5 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l} \text{All other} \\ \text{instructions} \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} \text{Less than} \\ 1.0 \end{array} & 35 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

When program [latex]\text{P}[/latex] is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation:
There is a single, shared EX-stage functional unit; only one instruction can occupy the EX stage per clock cycle (of duration [latex]1[/latex] ns). If an instruction's actual execution time [latex]t_{EX}[/latex] exceeds [latex]1[/latex] ns, it must occupy the EX stage for [latex]\lceil t_{EX}\rceil[/latex] clock cycles, causing [latex]\left(\lceil t_{EX}\rceil-1\right)[/latex] structural-hazard stall cycles for every instance of that instruction type.

[latex]\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}\text{Type}&t_{EX}&\text{cycles needed}&\text{stalls}\times M\\\hline\text{LOAD}&1.8&2&1\times15=15\\\text{IMUL}&1.5&2&1\times10=10\\\text{IDIV}&2.5&3&2\times5=10\\\text{FADD}&1.7&2&1\times10=10\\\text{FSUB}&1.7&2&1\times5=5\\\text{FMUL}&2.8&3&2\times15=30\\\text{FDIV}&3.2&4&3\times5=15\\\text{Others}&{<}1.0&1&0\times35=0\end{array}[/latex]

Total stall cycles [latex]=15+10+10+10+5+30+15+0=95[/latex].

Answer: 95

- [latex]i=1[/latex] (in that child): it forks again → this process (now acting as parent of its own fork) breaks (2nd process reaches printf); its own child continues.
- [latex]i=2[/latex] (in that grandchild): forks again → this one breaks (3rd process reaches printf); its child continues.
- [latex]i=3[/latex] (in the great-grandchild): loop condition [latex]i<3[/latex] fails, so the loop ends naturally without another fork (4th process reaches printf).

So exactly [latex]4[/latex] distinct processes each execute the [latex]\text{printf}[/latex] statement exactly once.

Answer: 4

question_text:
When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.'

If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: (A) If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
(B) When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
(C) If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.

- "If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room" is exactly the logical contrapositive of the original statement, so it is guaranteed true.
- "When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent" follows directly, since "standing [latex]\wedge[/latex] silent" implies "silent" alone. Guaranteed true.
- "When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing" similarly follows, since the conjunction implies "standing" alone. Guaranteed true.
- "If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room" is the converse of part of the original implication — the original statement never claims anything about what causes students to stand; they could be standing for a completely different reason (a fire alarm, another activity, etc.) while the teacher is absent. Answer: "If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room" is NOT necessarily true.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
For two different persons [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], the predicate [latex]M(x, y)[/latex] denotes that [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex].
Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?
options: (A) [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
(B) [latex](\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
(C) [latex](\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
(D) [latex](\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
explanation:
We need to translate: "There is a person [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]y[/latex] doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows [latex]y[/latex]."

- "There is a person [latex]y[/latex]" → [latex](\exists y)[/latex].
- "for every other person [latex]x[/latex] ([latex]x\ne y[/latex])" → [latex](\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)[/latex].
- "[latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex]" (everyone else knows this person) → [latex]M(x,y)[/latex].
- "[latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex]" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → [latex]\neg M(y,x)[/latex].

Combining: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)[/latex] — there exists such a special person [latex]y[/latex], and for every other person [latex]x[/latex], [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex] but [latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex].

The other options either use [latex]\forall y[/latex] (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use [latex]\exists x[/latex] (existentially quantifying [latex]x[/latex] instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

Answer: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\left((x\neq y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\right)[/latex]

question_text:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] decides the language [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex]
options: (A) Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] halts on all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex]

Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]."

The probability density function [latex]f(x)[/latex] of a random variable [latex]X[/latex] which takes real values is

subject: Compiler Design
question_text: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?
options: (A) A static variable declared inside a function
(B) An array of integers declared inside a function
(C) A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call
explanation:
In the C runtime memory model:

- A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap.
- A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack.
- The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame.
- Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called).

Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc()

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
explanation:
S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true.

S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false.

subject: Compiler Design
question_text:
Consider the following three ANSI-C programs, [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P1} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P2} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P3} \\ \hline \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} \\ \begin{array}{l} \text{int a=5;} \\ \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{float a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} \\ {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: (A) Only [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] will compile without any error
(B) Only [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] will compile without any error
(C) Only [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error
(D) All three programs [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error
explanation:
P1: Global [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] and, inside [latex]\text{main()}[/latex], a separate local [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex]. This is perfectly legal C — the local declaration simply shadows the global one within [latex]\text{main}[/latex]'s scope. Compiles fine.

P2: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed immediately by [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex] in the same block/scope — this is an illegal redeclaration of the same identifier [latex]a[/latex] within one scope, which is a compile-time error.

P3: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed by [latex]\text{float a=7;}[/latex] — again redeclaring [latex]a[/latex] in the same scope, this time with a conflicting type, which is also a compile-time error.

Answer: Only P1 will compile without any error.

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions [latex]T 1[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] in a DBMS, both of which access a data object [latex]A[/latex]. For these two transactions to not conflict on [latex]A[/latex], which one of the following statements must be true?
explanation:
Two operations by different transactions on the same data object [latex]A[/latex] "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome.

The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex].

Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A.

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
Consider a file of size [latex]4[/latex] million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth [latex]2[/latex] Mbps , [latex]500[/latex] kbps , and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.

Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?
Note: [latex]1 {M}=10^{6}, 1 {k}=10^{3}[/latex]
explanation:
With processing and propagation delays negligible, the effective throughput of a series of links is limited by the slowest (bottleneck) link in the path — here, [latex]500[/latex] kbps (since it's the minimum of [latex]2[/latex] Mbps, [latex]500[/latex] kbps, and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps).

File size [latex]=4\times10^6[/latex] bytes [latex]=4\times10^6\times8=32\times10^6[/latex] bits.

Total transfer time [latex]=\dfrac{32\times10^6\text{ bits}}{500\times10^3\text{ bps}}=64[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 64

subject: Computer Networks
question_text: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
explanation:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond.

[latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast.

Answer: DHCP

subject: Operating Systems
topic: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority)
question_text: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
explanation:
Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption:

- SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time.
- Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires.
- Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive.
- FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive.

subject: Algorithms
question_text:
Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer.

[latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex]

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?
Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
explanation:
Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]):

- [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial.
- [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself.
- [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex].
- [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]).

So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex].

Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!)

subject: Algorithms
question_text: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
explanation:
Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]:

- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms.

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text: Let [latex]R[/latex] be a binary relation on the set [latex]\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}[/latex], where [latex](x, y) \in R[/latex] if the product of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by [latex]R[/latex]?
explanation:
[latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square.

- Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds.
- Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds.
- Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds.
- Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails.

Answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive all hold (R is an equivalence relation); Antisymmetric does not hold.

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question_text: For a real number [latex]a[/latex], let [latex]I(a)=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(3 x^{2}-a x+1\right) d x[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: (A) The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] is independent of the value of [latex]a[/latex]
(B) The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] can vary with the value of [latex]a[/latex]
(C) There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number
(D) There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a negative real number
explanation:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx[/latex]

The middle term [latex]-ax[/latex] is an odd function of [latex]x[/latex], so its integral over the symmetric interval [latex][-1,1][/latex] is exactly [latex]0[/latex], regardless of the value of [latex]a[/latex]. Only the even part survives:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4[/latex]

So [latex]I(a)=4[/latex] for every real [latex]a[/latex] — the value is completely independent of [latex]a[/latex]. Since it's always [latex]4>0[/latex], there certainly exists (in fact, every) [latex]a[/latex] for which [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number; but there is no [latex]a[/latex] making it negative, and the value does not "vary."

Answer: I(a) is independent of a; and there exists a for which I(a) is positive (true for every a, since I(a)=4 always).

subject: Digital Logic
question_text: In a system, numbers are represented using [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement form. Consider four numbers [latex]N 1=1011, N 2=1101, N 3=1010[/latex] and [latex]N 4=1001[/latex] in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?
explanation:
Convert each 4-bit two's-complement number to its signed decimal value (invert bits and add [latex]1[/latex] if the leading bit is [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]N1{=}1011\to-5,\ N2{=}1101\to-3,\ N3{=}1010\to-6,\ N4{=}1001\to-7[/latex]. The representable range for [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement is [latex][-8,7][/latex]; a result falling outside this range signals overflow.

- [latex]N1+N2=-5+(-3)=-8[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N2+N3=-3+(-6)=-9[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.
- [latex]N3-N4=-6-(-7)=1[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N1+N4=-5+(-7)=-12[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.

Answer: N2+N3 and N1+N4 cause arithmetic overflow.

subject: Compiler Design
question_text: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?
explanation:
Checking each grammar for ambiguity (does some string have two distinct parse trees?):

- [latex]S\rightarrow aSb\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates only [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], with a unique nested derivation for every string — unambiguous.
- [latex]E\rightarrow E+E\mid E*E\mid id[/latex]: the classic textbook example of an ambiguous grammar — e.g. [latex]id+id*id[/latex] can be parsed with two different groupings (no precedence/associativity is encoded), giving two distinct parse trees.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid Sa\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates strings of [latex]a[/latex]'s only, but because both left-recursion ([latex]Sa[/latex]) and right-recursion ([latex]aS[/latex]) are available, a string like "[latex]aa[/latex]" can be built in more than one structurally distinct way — ambiguous.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid\epsilon[/latex]: purely right-recursive, unique derivation for every string — unambiguous.

Answer: [latex]E\rightarrow E+E|E*E|id[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow aS|Sa|\epsilon[/latex] are ambiguous.

subject: Engineering Mathematics
question_text:
Consider the system of linear equations given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{c} a x+y=b \\ 16 x+a y=24 \end{array} [/latex]

Suppose the values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation:
The system [latex]ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24[/latex] has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line, i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal:
[latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]

From [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}[/latex]: [latex]a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4[/latex].
From [latex]\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]: [latex]b=\dfrac{24}{a}[/latex].

If [latex]a=4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/4=6[/latex], so [latex]ab=4\times6=24[/latex].
If [latex]a=-4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/(-4)=-6[/latex], so [latex]ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24[/latex].

Either valid choice of [latex]a[/latex] gives the same product.

Answer: 24

subject: Algorithms
question_text:
Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of [latex]7[/latex] merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex].

The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation:
A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving.

Trace merge sort on [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]:

Bottom level (pairs):
[latex][10],[7]\to[7,10][/latex] (result is [latex]R[/latex] then [latex]L[/latex], not "[latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]") — not void.
[latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void.
[latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void.
[latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void.

Next level (quads):
[latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void.
[latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void.

Final merge:
[latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void.

Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void.

Answer: 3

subject: Algorithms
question_text:
Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
explanation:
The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees).

In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient.

Answer: 0

subject: Algorithms
question_text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
explanation:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary).

This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex]

question_text:
Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the condition given below.

[latex]\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}[/latex] such that [latex]i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])[/latex]

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
explanation:
The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex").

This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]

subject: Compiler Design
question_text:
Consider the canonical [latex]L R(0)[/latex] parsing of the grammar below using terminals [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex] and non-terminals [latex]\{A, B, C, S\}[/latex] with [latex]S[/latex] as the start symbol.

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow A C B \\ A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\ C \rightarrow c C \mid \epsilon \\ B \rightarrow b B \mid b \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the [latex]L R(0)[/latex] ACTION table?
explanation:
Building the LR(0) canonical collection for [latex]S\to ACB,\ A\to aA|\epsilon,\ C\to cC|\epsilon,\ B\to bB|b[/latex], a state has a shift-reduce conflict whenever it contains both a complete (reduce) item and a shift item on some terminal.

Tracing through the automaton, the following states each mix a reduce item with a shift item:
- The initial state [latex]\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot ACB,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The state reached after [latex]A[/latex], [latex]\{S\to A\cdot CB,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]a[/latex], [latex]\{A\to a\cdot A,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]c[/latex], [latex]\{C\to c\cdot C,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]b[/latex] (from [latex]B\to bB|b[/latex]), [latex]\{B\to b\cdot B,\ B\to b\cdot,\ B\to\cdot bB,\ B\to\cdot b\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]B\to b[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]b[/latex].

That gives exactly [latex]5[/latex] conflicting states (all other states, such as the ones after fully reducing [latex]A,C,B,[/latex] or [latex]S[/latex], contain only a single complete item and no competing shift).

Answer: 5

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex]
Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z
Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex]

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex]

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
explanation:
The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows:

1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]).
2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex].
3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity: [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex].

This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required).

Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity

subject: Computer Networks
question_text: Consider the transmission of data bits [latex]110001011[/latex] over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be [latex]1001[/latex], which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
explanation:
Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with [latex]3[/latex] zero bits appended, since the generator [latex]1001[/latex] has degree [latex]3[/latex]) by the generator [latex]1001[/latex], where each subtraction step is simply an XOR:

Dividend: [latex]110001011000[/latex] (original data [latex]110001011[/latex] followed by [latex]000[/latex]).
Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator [latex]1001[/latex] into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is [latex]1[/latex], and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder [latex]100[/latex].

This remainder [latex]100[/latex] is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword.

Answer: 100

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
explanation:
With [latex]16[/latex] general-purpose registers, each register operand needs [latex]\log_2 16=4[/latex] bits. The full instruction is [latex]2[/latex] bytes [latex]=16[/latex] bits.

- M-type: [latex]2[/latex] register operands ([latex]8[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate [latex]=14[/latex] bits of operand, leaving [latex]16-14=2[/latex] bits for the opcode → up to [latex]2^2=4[/latex] possible M-type codes, but only [latex]2[/latex] are actually used, leaving [latex]4-2=2[/latex] unused [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes free for other instruction types.
- R-type: [latex]3[/latex] register operands ([latex]12[/latex] bits), leaving [latex]16-12=4[/latex] bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix.
- C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. That single unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix expands into [latex]2^{6-4}=4[/latex] possible [latex]6[/latex]-bit C-type codes.

Answer: 4

subject: Database Management Systems
question_text:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index
[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation:
S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True.

S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true.

question_text:
Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: (D) [latex]\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}[/latex] consists of all strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]
explanation:
This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language).

Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex].

Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested).

Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3.

subject: Theory of Computation
question_text:
Let [latex]\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}[/latex] and let [latex]L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}[/latex].

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language [latex]L[/latex] is context-free?
explanation:
For [latex]L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}[/latex] with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other).

- [latex]i+k=j+\ell[/latex]: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ([latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]c[/latex]'s, which are not adjacent — [latex]b[/latex]'s and [latex]d[/latex]'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to [latex]a^nb^mc^nd^m[/latex] type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free.
- [latex]i=k[/latex] and [latex]j=\ell[/latex]: this needs matching [latex]a[/latex]'s to [latex]c[/latex]'s (skipping over the [latex]b[/latex]'s in between) AND separately matching [latex]b[/latex]'s to [latex]d[/latex]'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free.
- [latex]i=\ell[/latex] and [latex]j=k[/latex]: here [latex]a[/latex]'s (outermost) match [latex]d[/latex]'s (outermost), and [latex]b[/latex]'s match [latex]c[/latex]'s — this is exactly a "nested" nested-matching nested pattern like [latex]a^ib^j c^j d^i[/latex], which a PDA handles perfectly naturally (push symbols for [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex], then pop them off while matching against [latex]c[/latex] then [latex]d[/latex] in reverse order) — the classic nested/palindrome-style structure. Context-free.
- [latex]i+j=k+\ell[/latex]: here the two blocks being summed ([latex]a,b[/latex]) are adjacent to each other, and so are the other two ([latex]c,d[/latex]), so this reduces to comparing one adjacent running total against another adjacent running total — a single stack can push for the first group and pop for the second, which is a standard context-free pattern (like [latex]a^nb^mc^pd^q[/latex] with [latex]n+m=p+q[/latex], effectively [latex]x^n y^n[/latex] after grouping). Context-free.

Answer: i=ℓ and j=k; and i+j=k+ℓ, ensure L is context-free.

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text:
Consider a binary search tree (BST) with [latex]n[/latex] leaf nodes [latex](n>0)[/latex]. Given any node [latex]V[/latex], the key present in the node is denoted as [latex]{Val}(V)[/latex]. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers.

For a node [latex]V[/latex], let [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node [latex]V[/latex] does not have an inorder successor, then [latex]\operatorname{Suc}(V)[/latex] is [latex]N U L L[/latex]. As there are no duplicates, if [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] is not [latex]N U L L[/latex], then [latex]{Val}(V) < {Val}({Suc}(V))[/latex].

Corresponding to every leaf node [latex]L_{i}[/latex] that has a non-NULL [latex]\operatorname{Suc}\left(L_{i}\right)[/latex], a new key [latex]k_{i}[/latex] with the following property is to be inserted into the BST.

[latex] {Val}\left(L_{i}\right) < k_{i} < Val ({Suc}(L_{i}))[/latex]

Let [latex]K[/latex] represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST.

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: (B) [latex]K[/latex] will have at least one element
(C) After inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex], the height of the BST can increase at most by one
(D) Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex]
explanation:
Since inorder traversal visits keys in strictly increasing order, and [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between two consecutive values in that inorder sequence (a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] and its immediate successor), every such gap [latex](\text{Val}(L_i),\text{Val}(\text{Suc}(L_i)))[/latex] is a distinct, non-overlapping interval — so the chosen [latex]k_i[/latex] values can never coincide. K cannot have duplicates: True.

If the BST has only a single node (which is also its own only leaf, and is simultaneously the overall maximum so it has no inorder successor), then no leaf has a non-NULL successor at all, and [latex]K[/latex] would be empty. So [latex]K[/latex] having at least one element is not always true (fails for the trivial single-node tree).

Since each new key [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] (which has no children) and its successor, the standard BST insertion algorithm places [latex]k_i[/latex] directly as the right child of [latex]L_i[/latex] itself (since [latex]L_i[/latex] has no right subtree to begin with, being a leaf). This adds exactly one extra level below that specific leaf, so the overall tree height increases by at most [latex]1[/latex] (it stays the same unless one of the affected leaves was already at the maximum depth). True.

Since only leaves that have a non-NULL successor get a new key (not every single leaf, and definitely not every internal node), the total node count does not generally double. Not always true.

Answer: K cannot have duplicates; and after inserting all keys of K, the height increases by at most one.

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text:
Consider a stack [latex]S[/latex] and a queue [latex]Q[/latex]. Both of them are initially empty and have the capacity to store ten elements each. The elements [latex]1,2,3,4[/latex], and [latex]5[/latex] arrive one by one, in that order. When an element arrives, it is assigned either to [latex]S[/latex] (pushed on [latex]S[/latex] ) or to [latex]Q[/latex] (enqueued to [latex]Q[/latex] ). Once all the five elements are stored, the output is generated in two steps. First, stack S is emptied by popping all elements. Then queue [latex]Q[/latex] is emptied by dequeueing all elements. The output obtained by following this process is [latex]\text{4 3 1 2 5}[/latex].

Given the output, the objective is to predict whether an element was assigned to [latex]S[/latex] or [latex]Q[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are possible valid assignment(s) of the elements?
Note: In the options, the notation [latex]x S[/latex] denotes that element [latex]x[/latex] was assigned to [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]y Q[/latex] denotes that element [latex]y[/latex] was assigned to [latex]Q[/latex].
explanation:
The final output is: stack-popped elements first (in reverse of their push order), followed by queue-dequeued elements (in the same order they were enqueued). Target output: [latex]4,3,1,2,5[/latex].

Check each candidate by splitting into an [latex]S[/latex]-subsequence (in arrival order, then reversed for popping) and a [latex]Q[/latex]-subsequence (in arrival order, kept as-is):

- 1S,2Q,3S,4S,5Q: [latex]S[/latex] pushed in order [latex]1,3,4[/latex] → popped as [latex]4,3,1[/latex]. [latex]Q[/latex]: [latex]2,5[/latex]. Combined: [latex]4,3,1,2,5[/latex] — matches!
- 1Q,2Q,3S,4S,5Q: [latex]S[/latex] pushed [latex]3,4[/latex] → popped [latex]4,3[/latex]. [latex]Q[/latex]: [latex]1,2,5[/latex]. Combined: [latex]4,3,1,2,5[/latex] — matches!
- 1Q,2Q,3Q,4S,5S: [latex]S[/latex] pushed [latex]4,5[/latex] → popped [latex]5,4[/latex]. [latex]Q[/latex]: [latex]1,2,3[/latex]. Combined: [latex]5,4,1,2,3[/latex] — does not match.
- 1S,2S,3S,4Q,5Q: [latex]S[/latex] pushed [latex]1,2,3[/latex] → popped [latex]3,2,1[/latex]. [latex]Q[/latex]: [latex]4,5[/latex]. Combined: [latex]3,2,1,4,5[/latex] — does not match.

Answer: "1S,2Q,3S,4S,5Q" and "1Q,2Q,3S,4S,5Q" are both valid assignments.

subject: Operating Systems
explanation:
Semaphore [latex]A[/latex] (init [latex]1[/latex]) acts as a mutex guarding the critical section (print "*", increment [latex]X[/latex], and the [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] check), so all three processes enter this section one at a time, and exactly one of them (whichever happens to be the second to enter) will see [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] and print "[latex]\$[/latex]" then signal [latex]B[/latex]. Since the third process cannot even attempt this section until the second has released [latex]A[/latex] (which only happens after printing "[latex]\$[/latex]"), the global order is forced to always be: [latex]{*},{*},\$,{*}[/latex] — exactly two stars, then the dollar, then the third star. A pattern like [latex]{*}{*}{*}\$[/latex] (three stars before the dollar) can never occur.

After the dollar, semaphore [latex]B[/latex] gets exactly one initial permit, which starts a chain: each process that consumes the permit via [latex]\text{Wait}(B)[/latex] prints "[latex]\#[/latex]" and immediately regenerates the next permit via its own [latex]\text{Signal}(B)[/latex], letting the next process through in turn. The remaining ("third") star can interleave with this "[latex]\#[/latex]" chain at any point before that third process itself joins the chain — i.e. before any [latex]\#[/latex], after exactly one [latex]\#[/latex], or after exactly two [latex]\#[/latex]'s (but never after all three, since the third process must complete its own star/critical-section before it can take part in the [latex]\#[/latex] chain at all).

Answer: **$*###, **$#*##, and **$##*# are all possible; ***$### is impossible.

subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
question_text:
Consider a system with a processor and a [latex]4[/latex] KB direct mapped cache with block size of [latex]16[/latex] bytes. The system has a [latex]16[/latex] MB physical memory. Four words [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}[/latex], and S are accessed by the processor in the same order [latex]10[/latex] times. That is, there are a total of [latex]40[/latex] memory references in the sequence [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, {P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, \ldots[/latex]

Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below ([latex]1[/latex] word [latex]=1[/latex] byte).

[latex]\text{P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32}[/latex]

Which of the following statements is/are true?
Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]
options: (A) Every access to [latex]\text{P}[/latex] results in a cache miss
(B) Every access to [latex]\text{R}[/latex] results in a cache hit
(C) Every access to [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] results in a cache miss
(D) Except the first access to [latex]\text{S}[/latex], all subsequent accesses to [latex]\text{S}[/latex] result in cache hits
explanation:
Cache: [latex]4[/latex] KB, block size [latex]16[/latex] bytes [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] offset [latex]=4[/latex] bits, number of lines [latex]=4096/16=256=2^8\Rightarrow[/latex] index [latex]=8[/latex] bits; physical memory [latex]16[/latex] MB [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] address width [latex]=24[/latex] bits, so tag [latex]=24-8-4=12[/latex] bits.

Computing (block-address, index, tag) for each word shows that [latex]P=0\text{x}845B32[/latex] and [latex]R=0\text{x}845B36[/latex] fall in the same [latex]16[/latex]-byte block (both addresses lie within [latex]0\text{x}845B30[/latex]-[latex]0\text{x}845B3F[/latex]), while [latex]Q=0\text{x}845B26[/latex] maps to a different cache line (a different index) than [latex]P/R[/latex], and [latex]S=0\text{x}846B32[/latex] maps to the same index as [latex]P/R[/latex] but with a different tag (so [latex]S[/latex] conflicts with [latex]P/R[/latex]'s cache line).

Simulating the repeating access sequence [latex]P,Q,R,S,P,Q,R,S,\ldots[/latex]: each [latex]S[/latex] access evicts the [latex]P/R[/latex] block (same index, different tag), so the very next [latex]P[/latex] access is always a fresh miss (reloading [latex]P[/latex]'s block, which also brings in [latex]R[/latex] since they share a block); the following [latex]R[/latex] access is then always a hit (block was just loaded by [latex]P[/latex]); and the following [latex]S[/latex] access is always a miss again (conflicts with the just-refreshed [latex]P/R[/latex] tag). Meanwhile [latex]Q[/latex]'s index never conflicts with anything else, so only its very first access misses; all later [latex]Q[/latex] accesses are hits (not "every access misses").

Answer: Every access to P is a miss, and every access to R is a hit.
