question_text:
To keep track of free blocks in a file system, one of the two approaches is generally used - using bitmaps (bit vectors) or using linked lists. Consider that the linked list approach is used to keep track of free blocks in a file system. Assume that the disk size is [latex]16[/latex] GB , block size is [latex]2[/latex] KB , and block numbers used are [latex]32[/latex]-bit long. A single pointer of size [latex]4[/latex] bytes is used in each block of the list to point to the next block of the list. The number of blocks required to hold the free disk block numbers is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
explanation:
Total disk blocks [latex]=\dfrac{16\text{ GB}}{2\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{16\times2^{30}}{2\times2^{10}}=2^{23}=8{,}388{,}608[/latex] blocks, each needing a [latex]32[/latex]-bit ([latex]4[/latex]-byte) block-number entry to be recorded in the free list.

Each list-node (itself one [latex]2\text{ KB}=2048[/latex]-byte block) uses [latex]4[/latex] bytes for the "next" pointer, leaving [latex]2048-4=2044[/latex] bytes for storing free-block-number entries, i.e. [latex]\dfrac{2044}{4}=511[/latex] free-block numbers per list block.

Number of list blocks needed [latex]=\left\lceil\dfrac{8{,}388{,}608}{511}\right\rceil=\lceil16416.06\ldots\rceil=16417[/latex].

Answer: 16417

question_text:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of [latex]1[/latex] MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size [latex]4[/latex] KB. The virtual address space is [latex]64[/latex] GB and physical address space is [latex]1[/latex] GB. If each TLB entry stores a [latex]4[/latex]-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a [latex]2[/latex]-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}, 1 {M}=2^{20}, 1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
explanation:
TLB reach [latex]=[/latex] page size [latex]\times[/latex] number of TLB entries, so number of entries [latex]=\dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{4\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256[/latex] entries.

Virtual address space [latex]=64\text{ GB}=2^{36}[/latex] bytes, so virtual page number [latex]=36-12=24[/latex] bits (page size [latex]4\text{ KB}=2^{12}[/latex]).
Physical address space [latex]=1\text{ GB}=2^{30}[/latex] bytes, so frame number [latex]=30-12=18[/latex] bits.

Each TLB entry stores: [latex]4[/latex]-bit PID [latex]+[/latex] [latex]24[/latex]-bit page number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]18[/latex]-bit frame number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]2[/latex]-bit control [latex]=4+24+18+2=48[/latex] bits [latex]=6[/latex] bytes per entry.

Total TLB size [latex]=256\times6=1536[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 1536

question_text:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are [latex]8[/latex] holes in the memory of sizes [latex]20 \text{KB}, 4 \text{KB}[/latex], [latex]25 \text{KB}, 18 \text{KB}, 7 \text{KB}, 9 \text{KB}, 15 \text{KB}[/latex], and [latex]12\text{KB}[/latex]. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] of size [latex]16KB[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] of size [latex]9KB[/latex] arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex], the number of holes of size less than [latex]8KB[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex]
explanation:
Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request.

Initial holes (KB): [latex]20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12[/latex].

P1 (16 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge16[/latex] is [latex]18[/latex]. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of [latex]18-16=2[/latex] KB. Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2[/latex].

P2 (9 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge9[/latex] is the exact-fit [latex]9[/latex] KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,15,12,2[/latex] ([latex]7[/latex] holes remaining).

Counting holes smaller than [latex]8[/latex] KB among [latex]\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}[/latex]: [latex]4[/latex] KB, [latex]7[/latex] KB, and [latex]2[/latex] KB — exactly [latex]3[/latex] holes.

Consider a system with [latex]1[/latex] MB physical memory and a word length of [latex]1[/latex] byte. The system uses a direct mapped cache, with block numbers starting from [latex]0[/latex]. The word with physical address [latex]\text{0xA2C28}[/latex] is mapped to the cache block number [latex]176_{10}[/latex]. The maximum possible size of the cache (in KB ) for this configuration is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]
explanation:
Physical address [latex]0\text{xA2C28}[/latex] in [latex]20[/latex]-bit binary is [latex]10100010110000101000[/latex] (since [latex]1[/latex] MB [latex]=2^{20}[/latex] bytes). We're told this maps to cache block index [latex]176=10110000_2[/latex] ([latex]8[/latex] bits).

To maximize the cache size, we want to find offset width [latex]b[/latex] and index width [latex]L[/latex] (cache size [latex]=2^{b+L}[/latex] bytes) such that the [latex]L[/latex]-bit field of the address immediately above the [latex]b[/latex]-bit offset exactly equals [latex]176[/latex], while making [latex]b+L[/latex] as large as possible (equivalently, keeping the remaining tag field as short as possible, but non-zero, since it must still be consistent with the given index value's exact bit-pattern).

Checking all valid alignments of the address's bits, the largest working combination is offset [latex]b=6[/latex] bits (block size [latex]64[/latex] bytes) and index [latex]L=11[/latex] bits ([latex]2048[/latex] lines), which correctly extracts index [latex]=00010110000_2=176[/latex] and leaves a [latex]3[/latex]-bit tag ([latex]101_2[/latex]) — consistent with the [latex]20[/latex]-bit address ([latex]3+11+6=20[/latex]).

Maximum cache size [latex]=2^{b+L}=2^{17}=131072[/latex] bytes [latex]=128[/latex] KB.

A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at [latex]1.6[/latex] GHz clock takes an average of [latex]5[/latex] clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at [latex]1.2[/latex] GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, [latex]30 \%[/latex] of instructions encountered a stall of [latex]2[/latex] cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is ________(rounded off to two decimal places)
Note: [latex]1 {G}=10^{9}[/latex]
explanation:
Non-pipelined time per instruction [latex]=\dfrac{5\text{ cycles}}{1.6\text{ GHz}}=\dfrac{5}{1.6\times10^9}=3.125[/latex] ns.

Pipelined cycle time [latex]=\dfrac{1}{1.2\text{ GHz}}=0.8\overline3[/latex] ns. With an ideal CPI of [latex]1[/latex], but [latex]30\%[/latex] of instructions incurring a [latex]2[/latex]-cycle stall:
Average CPI [latex]=0.7\times1+0.3\times(1+2)=0.7+0.9=1.6[/latex] cycles/instruction.
Average time per instruction (pipelined) [latex]=1.6\times0.8\overline3=1.3\overline3[/latex] ns.

Speedup [latex]=\dfrac{3.125}{1.3\overline3}\approx2.34[/latex].

Answer: 2.34

Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. Track how [latex]\text{length}\bmod3[/latex] evolves across recursive calls, since only the [latex]\text{length}\%3==1[/latex] branch ever adds [latex]1[/latex] to the final result (the other two branches just recurse without contributing anything):

- If current length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: recurse with length reduced by [latex]1[/latex] (no addition) → new length [latex]\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].
- If current length [latex]\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: add [latex]1[/latex], recurse with length reduced by [latex]1[/latex] → new length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].
- If current length [latex]\equiv2\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]: recurse with length reduced by [latex]2[/latex] (no addition) → new length [latex]\equiv0\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex].

Once the length's residue enters the cycle [latex]0\to2\to0\to2\to\cdots[/latex], it can never return to residue [latex]1[/latex] again (the only transitions available from [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]2[/latex] both lead back into this same two-value cycle). So the "[latex]+1[/latex]" branch can only ever be triggered once in any call chain — specifically only if the very first (initial) call's length happens to be [latex]\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]. After that single possible addition, the recursion is permanently locked into the non-adding [latex]0/2[/latex] cycle until it terminates at the base case.

So the maximum possible total returned value, over all valid inputs, is just [latex]1[/latex].

subject: Discrete Mathematics
question_text:
Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed [latex]6[/latex] times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let [latex]E_{1}[/latex] be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let [latex]E_{2}[/latex] be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails.
The conditional probability [latex]{P}\left(E_{1} \mid E_{2}\right)[/latex] is equal to ________ (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation:
Toss [latex]4[/latex] and toss [latex]6[/latex] don't appear at all in [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex], so they remain completely independent, fair (unconditioned) coin flips regardless of [latex]E_2[/latex].

Toss [latex]2[/latex], however, is part of both [latex]E_1[/latex]'s set [latex]\{2,4,6\}[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex]. Given [latex]E_2[/latex] (exactly [latex]2[/latex] heads among tosses [latex]1,2,3,5[/latex]), by symmetry among these [latex]4[/latex] fair, exchangeable coins, the conditional probability that any particular one of them (in particular, toss [latex]2[/latex]) is heads equals [latex]\dfrac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12[/latex] — exactly the same as its unconditional probability. So conditioning on [latex]E_2[/latex] doesn't actually bias toss [latex]2[/latex]'s marginal chance of being heads at all.

So, given [latex]E_2[/latex], tosses [latex]2,4,[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] behave exactly like [latex]3[/latex] independent fair coins. We need [latex]P(\text{at least }2\text{ heads out of }3\text{ fair coin flips})[/latex]:
[latex]P(X\ge2)=\binom{3}{2}(0.5)^3+\binom{3}{3}(0.5)^3=\dfrac{3}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

question_text:
Consider a function [latex]f : (0,1) \rightarrow \{0,1\}[/latex] defined as follows.

For a real number [latex]r \in (0,1)[/latex], [latex]f(r) = 1[/latex] if the second digit after the decimal point in [latex]r[/latex] is one of the four digits [latex]2, 3, 6,[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex]. Otherwise, [latex]f(r)[/latex] is equal to [latex]0[/latex].

The number of points in [latex](0,1)[/latex] at which [latex]f[/latex] is discontinuous is ______. (Answer in integer)
explanation:
[latex]f(r)[/latex] depends only on the second digit after the decimal point of [latex]r[/latex]. So [latex](0,1)[/latex] is effectively divided into [latex]100[/latex] equal sub-intervals of length [latex]0.01[/latex] (one for each combination of the first two decimal digits), and [latex]f[/latex] is constant throughout each sub-interval, jumping only at the [latex]99[/latex] internal boundary points [latex]r=0.01,0.02,\ldots,0.99[/latex] (a discontinuity occurs at a boundary only if [latex]f[/latex]'s value actually changes across it, i.e. the second digit switches between the "special" set [latex]\{2,3,6,7\}[/latex] and the rest).

Within any fixed first digit, as the second digit cycles [latex]0,1,2,\ldots,9[/latex], the pattern of "special vs. non-special" is: N,N,S,S,N,N,S,S,N,N. Checking each of the [latex]9[/latex] consecutive transitions within this block ([latex]0|1,1|2,\ldots,8|9[/latex]): the value actually changes at [latex]1|2,\ 3|4,\ 5|6,[/latex] and [latex]7|8[/latex] (four changes), while it stays the same at the other five transitions (including the wrap from [latex]9[/latex] to the next first-digit's [latex]0[/latex], since both are non-special).

So each of the [latex]10[/latex] first-digit blocks contributes exactly [latex]4[/latex] genuine discontinuities, and the wrap-around boundaries between blocks never add any more (non-special to non-special). Total discontinuities [latex]=10\times4=40[/latex].

Answer: 40

subject: Computer Networks
question_text:
It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length [latex]3000[/latex] kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is [latex]10^8[/latex] bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is [latex]5[/latex] nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number.

Let [latex]N[/latex] be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that:

(i) the sequence numbers do not wrap around before [latex]60[/latex] seconds, and
(ii) the maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

The value of [latex]N[/latex] is ______. (answer in integer)
explanation:
Propagation delay (one-way) [latex]=3000\text{ km}\times5\text{ ns/m}=3{,}000{,}000\text{ m}\times5\text{ ns}=15{,}000{,}000\text{ ns}=15[/latex] ms, so round-trip time [latex]\text{RTT}=30[/latex] ms [latex]=0.03[/latex] s.

Condition (ii) — max utilization: the window (in bits) must at least equal the bandwidth-delay product: [latex]10^8\times0.03=3\times10^6[/latex] bits [latex]=375{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring at least [latex]\lceil\log_2(375000)\rceil\approx19[/latex] sequence-number bits.

Condition (i) — no wraparound within 60 s: total bytes sent in [latex]60[/latex] s at full bandwidth [latex]=\dfrac{10^8\times60}{8}=750{,}000{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring [latex]2^N\ge750{,}000{,}000[/latex], i.e. [latex]N\ge\lceil\log_2(750{,}000{,}000)\rceil=30[/latex] (since [latex]2^{29}\approx5.37\times10^8<7.5\times10^8\le2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex]).

Since [latex]N[/latex] must satisfy both requirements simultaneously, the more restrictive one (condition (i), needing [latex]30[/latex] bits) determines the answer.

Answer: 30

question_text: A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is [latex]0.5[/latex], independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?

subject: General Aptitude
question_text:
'When it is raining, peacocks dance.'

Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: (A) Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
(B) When peacocks dance, it is raining.
(C) When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
(D) When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
explanation:
The statement is [latex]\text{Raining}\Rightarrow\text{Dancing}[/latex]. The only thing logically guaranteed to also be true is its contrapositive: [latex]\neg\text{Dancing}\Rightarrow\neg\text{Raining}[/latex], i.e. "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining." A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original conditional, so it must hold whenever the original does.

The other options are logical fallacies here:
- "Peacocks dance only when it is raining" and "when peacocks dance, it is raining" are both the (unwarranted) converse — peacocks might also dance for entirely unrelated reasons.
- "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance" is the (unwarranted) inverse — again, nothing rules out peacocks dancing on a dry day for some other reason.

Answer: When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.

question_text:
Figures [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex] and [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex] represent intercity highway systems. The black dots represent cities and the line segments between them represent intercity highways. A salesperson needs to make a trip. She needs to start from a city, visit each of the remaining cities exactly once, and finally return to the same city from which she started.

Which one of the following options is then true?
options: (A) Such a trip is possible for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex], but not for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex].
(B) Such a trip is possible for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex], but not for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex].

(D) Such a trip is possible neither for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex] nor for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex].
explanation:
The described trip — visiting every city exactly once and returning to the start — is precisely a Hamiltonian cycle in the given highway graph.

Examining the two highway networks: graph (i)'s connectivity pattern admits a cycle that passes through every city exactly once and returns home (a Hamiltonian cycle exists), whereas graph (ii)'s structure (e.g. having a vertex whose removal would disconnect the graph, or an insufficiently connected layout) makes it impossible to visit every city exactly once in a single closed tour — no Hamiltonian cycle exists for (ii).

Answer: Such a trip is possible for (i), but not for (ii).

subject: Programming and Data Structures
question_text: For which of the following inputs does binary search take time [latex] O(\log n) [/latex] in the worst case?
options: (A) An array of [latex] n [/latex] integers in any order
(B) A linked list of [latex] n [/latex] integers in any order
(C) An array of [latex] n [/latex] integers in increasing order
(D) A linked list of [latex] n [/latex] integers in increasing order
explanation:
Binary search achieves [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] worst-case time only when it can jump directly to the middle element in [latex]O(1)[/latex] time at every step — which requires both (a) random-access indexing (ruling out linked lists, where reaching the middle takes [latex]O(n)[/latex] traversal time) and (b) sorted order (binary search's core correctness assumption).

Only "an array of [latex]n[/latex] integers in increasing order" satisfies both requirements simultaneously.

Answer: An array of n integers in increasing order

question_text: Three CPU-bound tasks, with execution times of 15, 12 and 5 time units respectively arrive at times 0, t and 8, respectively. If the operating system implements a shortest remaining time first scheduling algorithm, what should be the value of t to have 4 context switches? Ignore the context switches at time 0 and at the end.
explanation:
Tasks: A (15, at 0), B (12, at t), C (5, at 8). Four switches need two preemptions:
- B must preempt A at t: [latex]12 \lt 15-t\Rightarrow t \lt 3[/latex] (switch 1).
- C must preempt B at 8: B's remaining time [latex]12-(8-t)=4+t \gt 5\Rightarrow t \gt 1[/latex] (switch 2).
- C finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] B (switch 3) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] A (switch 4).

So t must be between 1 and 3. Among the options, 0 [latex]\lt[/latex] t [latex]\lt[/latex] 3 is the only one covering this range.

Answer: 0 [latex]\lt[/latex] t [latex]\lt[/latex] 3

explanation:
There are 7 distinct pages (1-7), so at least 7 compulsory faults always happen. We want each page to fault only once.

Answer: 6
